speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
House in committee on Bill 133, The WaT-Time Elections Act, Mr. W. H. Bennett in the Chair.
On section 1-Part 1 of Dominion Elections Act suspended' and part 2 to operate as amended:

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I suggest that we consider the Bill panagragh by paragraph. Section l occupies about 10 pages, and the matters referred to are not alike in character.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I do not see that there would be very much value in reading the whole section. We might consider it as much as possible in the order in which it appears. I know that it is impossible to confine the discussion to any particular clause of the Bill. We may take the discussion on the whole clause, but commence with the first part of it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I desire to call attention to the words "complete demobilization" which appear in this Bill and in former Acts. That expression has never been given any legal definition. What is complete demobilization? Mobilization is simply calling the forces together, and demobilization will mean the time when, after peace is concluded, the order is given to recall the troops. Unless we have a definite definition, the period of demobilization may be extended to an unknown length.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I think demobilization
has a distinct significance.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: What is it?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I am not able to give
it accurately, but my opinion of it is this: complete demobilization takes place when all those enlisted in the Canadian Expeditionary Forces are released from further obligations as members thereof.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I remind the Secretary
of State that judicial decisions were given in England after the South African war defining the period of demobilization. I think they may have something to do with the names of the men being placed on the voters' lists.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Those decisions will
apply here.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Perhaps my hon. friend
could get information on the subject and give it to the committee.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I shall try to get it.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Do I understand that a
definition is to be given of complete demobilization?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I do not think that a
definition is necessary in the Act. I stated that I would ascertain what the legal sig

nificance of it was, as determined by British decisions, and that I would inform the committee. In the absence of any Canadian decisions the English decisions would be followed.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Does this legislation
apply to by-elections held after the general election?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
If by-elections were
held prior to demobilization, the provisions of this Bill would apply, because the Dominion Elections Act as it stands now applies to by-elections as well as to general elections. This Bill suspends the operation of certain clauses of the Dominion Elections Act and makes it read in a certain way until a certain time. Consequently, this Act, during the period of its operation, would apply to by-elections.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: In that case, having regard to the provisions of the Military Voters' Act, at every by-election every one of the thousands of men who are Britisn subjects and who never lived in Canada would have a vote. A great deal of expense would be incurred in taking the votes of the soldiers overseas at every by-election.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The Military Voters' Act does not apply to by-elections. If it be decided to hold by-elections after the general election, some new provisions will have to be made, because we c<^uld not take the soldiers' votes in a by-election. I quite agree that the provisions of this Bill would be very awkward of application in such oases. It was not intended that this Act should apply to by-elections, but legally it would.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: No matter what party succeeds in the coming contest, by-elections will be necessary prior to the meeting of Parliament. Nearly always after an election some additional persons are called into the Government, or some defeated minister has to find a seat. The probability of this occurring within the next few months is more marked than it ever would be under normal conditions.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
It is difficult enough to provide for a general election in war time; we hope to avoid the necessity of providing for a by-election. I can conceive of scarce-

ly anything more impracticable than to hold a by-election fairly in war time. It would be a tremendous task to pick out the soldiers who should vote in a particular constituency, to ascertain what relatives should vote in that district, and so on. I think the best way to avoid that would be not to have any'ministers defeated.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: You had better put that in the Bill.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: That is not a bad idea.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The law is that newly appointed ministers who formerly were ordinary members of Parliament must be re-elected. I suggest that i' be provided tlut members of the Opposition who are elected and afterwards made ministers of the Crown shall not have to be re-elected.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I call the attention of the committee to the fact that part 4 of the Military Voters' Act applies only in the event of a general election.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: "The Dominion Elections Act" is the title of our present law. This Bill might well be styled "The War Time. Dominion Elections Act."

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Does the Secretary of State not think it advisable to make this law applicable only to general elections?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I cannot say that that would be advisable. If by-elections are held, some law must be applicable-some law that will enable the vote to be recorded. However awkward the application of this Act might be, it would be better than the application of the other Act, which would be a downright outrage in a by-election. Before we are out of committee, I think consideration had better be given to the subject of by-election.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Why not insert a provision stating that the law shall apply only to general elections?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I will give consideration to that. But the effect of that would be this: in one province I do not think a by-election could be held at all. If a byelection could be held in a given province, it would be on a different basis entirely fiom that on which a general election is held. However, I will see whether less trouble would be given by making the law apply to general elections only. That provision will be adopted which will create the less trouble and be the more equitable.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
What is the affect of a
and b in this section?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The effect-my words apply to similar clauses all through the Bill-is to make the list-making provisions now applicable in part 2 to Alberta and Saskatchewan, applicable generally throughout Canada.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Is this part of the clause
to be adopted? Surely that part which relates to demobilization cannot be adopted if the Government is going to give the matter consideration.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: What I stated was that I would give the legal interpretation of the word as decided in the court. The paragraph stands so far as that is concerned.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
The Act should stand, not only for that purpose, but for the purpose of deciding whether you are going to make it effective after the general election is held or not, because that question is linked up with the other. The minister was to state whether or not this Act would cease to be effective at the close of the general election.
( -^r MEIGHEN:	The paragraph will
stand.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I have not the advantage of being a member of the legal profession, and, therefore, I am not as well able to dovetail this amending Act into the original Act as those who 'are of that profession. I find the greatest difficulty in arriving at an understanding of ithe provisions of this amending Act on account of having .to do so much dovetailing with the original Act. Would it not have been possible to draw up this amending Act as a whole, that is to say, to make it complete in itself with such provisions as would be necessary in order to leave the original Act 'as it stands, but so that the citizen who was not a member of the .legal profession could have some reasonable idea of the working and the effect of the new provisions? I am unable to follow intelligently .the provisions of this new Bill.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: That was my trouble.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The Bill will be printed as amended immediately Parliament decides how it should be .amended. For the purpose of the committee now, I may say that the Bill will read in this way generally: The first four clauses of the old Act will remain as they are, that is, the sections before we come to Part I. The first section

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: defines the Act as the Dominion Elections Act. The -second, section gives the definitions ,and interpretations. The third -section states that no one can be a candidate unless his consent is given. The fourth section requires the presence of -agents. Those -stand a-s -they are. Then everything in Part I is struck out until we come to 32.
You are striking that -out.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes, but we are substituting another section. When we come to section 32, we strike it out, for the reason that section 32 defines the old qualifications in Alberta -and Saskatchewan. That is] the qualifications of voters fixed by the Dominion Parliament is applicable to those provinces. This Bill takes the provincial qualifications in those provinces exactly the same as in those other provinces. Consequently we take section 10, which was in Part I, and we substitute that for the old section 32. The present section 32 on the first page of the Bill is- section 10 of the old Act.
Will the Secretary of State secure a dozen or two dozen copies of the Act as -amended for distribution?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I have just managed to get one compiled for myself. I show to the committee the size that it is.

Has the minister copies of the old Act as printed before, so that we can follow the amendments? .
*

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I had that done. I had a large number of copies of the old Act set up for distribution.

I cannot find
them.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not know where they are. I thought hon. members had them.
When was that done?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Four days ago.
I was unable to get one.
I applied to the Printing Bureau on my own account, and I secured two copies.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I asked that copies be sent to the distribution office for the table of the House.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Copies of the Dominion Elections Act, with all the amendments up to date, will be distributed.

An ordinary man would lose himself amongst all the amendments. For a man like myself it is very hard to understand the whole thing. I would suppose, that a -gentleman like the Secretary of State, with all his- talents and capacity and with all the workers at his disposal, could have presented, us with a Bill complete by itself without any reference to the old Act. In a few days more he could have given to the committee a complete Bill -that hon. .members and the general public could understand. I defy anybody to understand this measure. I have already heard the most talented lawyers complaining that they cannot understand one bit of it. Would it not be a good thing to adjourn this debate until the Government-and I refer in particular to the Solicitor General, with his talent- draw up a measure that the Government would understand?
Oh.

Hon. gentlemen opposite may laugh. I defy hon. gentlemen opposite, except possibly the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General who may understand the Bill, to tell us what it means. They are at sea just as I am in regard to this legislation, but they will vote for it no matter whether they understand it or not. I beg tlie Government, and especially the Secretary of State, to frame a law so that the ordinary citizen of this country will understand it. Is this a trap? I want to find that out. I do not believe so; I believe the Secretary of State is honest in this respect, but the Government should not play with the people as they are doing by this piece of paper. By the first section the minister strikes out sections 1 to 31 of the Dominion Elections Act. Does any hon. member know if he has struck out enough or too much? Then after section 32 everything is upset, and the Secretary of State takes the precaution of saying: When we enact a section between sections 33 and 34, it is section 33A. I am in earnest in asking that a measure be framed so that tihe general public will be able to understand it,



and with the capacity of our hon. friends, that should be done in a day or two. In Quebec, when we amend an Act, we have to repeat the whole section that is amended. We do not only say that we strike out section 5 and replace it by section 4, but we repeat the whole section, and we put the new matter in brackets so that we know exactly where we stand. What I am asking for the people of this country, and especially for the people of my constituency, is that we should have a law that we can comprehend.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada

speechtext:
I have gone carefully
over the Bill and I quite agree with the Solicitor General that as discussion proceeds we shall begin to understand it more and more, and in the end -it will no doubt be pretty clear to us. But the ordinary man reading this Bill finds it very difficult lo understand.

What do you
mean by the ordinary man?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: We are a long way from: those clauses of the Bill as yet.

No, you are not, because the moment you strike out the heading, " Provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta and Yukon Territory " you make the law applicable to the whole of Canada, which, of course, includes those provinces^ where they have the provincial lists.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
We must have some
means of getting these names on the lists. The hon. gentleman suggests that we have some short clausees in the Bill providing for it. That is just what we have. The quickest way to do it is to make it the business of somebody to get it done, and that is	what we have done. It
is true	that	a great, many new
names will have to added, but very few names in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, for instance, will have to be struck off, and unless we make it somebody's business to look after the enrolling of these new names they will never get on in time. You cannot make it the business of judges to go over the length and breadth of these counties, if we are to have an election in reasonable time. The method has worked fairly well in the western provinces. There has been complaint that there were no safeguards for the Opposition, that the enumerators appointed by the Government in power had an advantage. But we have given safeguards here that are just as much to the advantage of one side as the other.
I have not been able to discover many safeguards.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not know of a more expeditious or simpler method of getting the additional votes that we have provided.

In the rural constituencies of the province of Quebec the lists are prepared by the secretary-treasurer for the municipality. He is the man who prepares the assessment roll and knows everybody in the municipality, and he acts under the control of the local municipal council. The lists are prepared by him and transmitted to tne registrar of the county, and by him sent forward to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, and eventually they become the official lists. Speaking for my own constituency, of which I have more particular knowledge, I know that the minister will be unable to find in any parish or township ;t man better qualified to prepare these lists than the secretary-treasurer of the municipality. He has the advantage of having all the information he needs in his hands. There will be no question of politics in it, because in one municipality the secretary-treasurer might be a Conservative, and in the next a Liberal. I certainly think this 357H
officer would he the best man that could be got.
It is the same in the province of New Brunswick.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: If you do that it simply means that you are making them enumerators.
Why not make them enumerators? They are the very best men you can get?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I am not so sure of that. If we use the machinery that is now in the provinces, the length of time that the Quebec law allows would lengthen out the whole contest. Furthermore, you have to have men who make it their business to understand this law. It is their peculiar business to find out who is entitled to vote under this law and then to put their names on the list. I do not know any reason why municipal officers would be the proper men in Quebec, when all along, ever since 1905, special officers have been appointed for the purpose in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. They have never used the secretary-treasurer of the municipalities there. Personally, I think the secretary-treasurers would resent very much having this made a part of their duties.

In the newer provinces we have, and shall have for a certain number of years, a shifting population. There are many residents of the United States who own large tracts of land in Canada. As was explained to me by an hon. friend from the West last night, municipal government in the West is as yet only in embryo.
My hon. friend from Ronaventure (Mr. Marcil) sayis we have an old settled population in the province of Quebec. That is perfectly true. Everybody knows everybody else. The municipal officer is a trusted official of the municipality; he acts on the school commission; he is clerk of the justices of the peace, and so on; he is secretary-treasurer of the municipality, .and generally speaking he attends to all public functions in the municipality; he knows everybody; he knows the Topes, so 'to speak.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: What would be the population of some of your larger munici-. palities?

The population varies; it would be anywhere from 300, 400, or 500 up to 1,000, or, perhaps, 1,500. I can assure my hon. friend that, if he will look into the matter he will find that the muni-

cipal officer is the best and moat trusted officer in the municipality, and I daresay, fox a small remuneration, better work could * be got from him than if a stranger were brought in from the city, or if you were to appoint a lawyer from the shire town. I can assure my hon. friend that the municipal officer would give better satisfaction to the public. He knows every man, woman and child in the community, and if you avail yourself of his services I am satisfied you will find it much more convenient.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The isiz-e of the municipality, if nothing else, makes it impracticable.
What do you mean by that?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The population ,and the extent of the municipality. The scheme of this Act is that the work shall be done quickly by a large staff of officers who are paid a reasonable amount for their work. You cannot have it extended over a great length of time.

If my 'hon. friend will allow me, if you utilize the services of those municipal officers in the parishes and in the villages, and then have one enumerator for each constituency or each county, those municipal officers could report to the chief enumerator. But, to reach the people, to know the people and to enumerate them, no better means could be adopted than to avail ourselves of the services of these municipal officers.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend has '
not quite seized the scheme yet. It woulti not do to have a municipal officer to take charge of all those in the municipality. An enumerator is responsible for a single polling division, and there must be one enumerator for each division, because he must sit at a certain place near the poll, for ten days before the voting, and he must sit at the poll or close to it on the polling day, so that if a man is not on the list he may go there and get a certificate to vote, or a certificate of refusal. It is true the lists compiled by these municipal officers will be used, and these lists are final as far as they go.
Are they final? As 1 read the Act the enumerator can strike off or add to the list according to his own judgment.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend is wrong. The intention is that in Ontario, *Quebec, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia,
[Mr. Lemieux.J
the enumerator cannot touch the list except for two [DOT] purposes-he can strike off but only for alienage, he can add to, but only fox tlhe female relatives of soldiers.
I do not so read it. If my hon. friend's statement is correct, it would be an improvement.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: That is the intention, and if it is not clear in the Act it will be made clear.

While the provisions for compiling the voters' lists in the prairie provinces have been suitable and applicable to the conditions in those provinces, the reason is because there were peculiar conditions to be met, and the fact that the method adopted there was the best available method does mot by any means settle the question that it is the best available method for other and entirely different conditions. The work of an enumerator in compiling the lists there was necessary because of what might be called the fluid character of the population, and the widely scattered settlements. It was the only way to arrive at any sort of knowledge as to who should or who should not vote. The method was not adopted because it was the best way to secure a sound and proper voters' list, and as a matter of fact it has not been found to be a good way where population is dense in the prairie provinces. It is not a good way in the cities, for instance. It is, however, the best method available in the scattered outlying rural 'settlements. While I aim not sufficiently versed with conditions in this part of the country to criticise the Bill as applied to conditions here, I merely wish to point out for the information of the committee that the reason this system, is used in the West is because of the peculiar conditions existing there, and not because the method is inherently or necessarily the best. I know of cases where an enumerator covers more than one polling division in the West, the reason being that the population is	so very scattered that it
would	be unjust	to include the
total area in one poll, because it would be too far for the people to travel and at tlhe same time it would not be worth while to appoint an enumerator for the small population voting at a single poll. Those are conditions peculiar to that country. Another point is that in regard to the actual casting of the vote, the fact that a man can swear his vote on, as we say, does not render the amendment of the list by the enumerator a serious matter there.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The feature that has existed of enabling one enumerator to act in more than one polling division in sparse populations is eliminated in this Bill. Otherwise, you could not carry out the provisions of the Bill, The enumerator must be there in order to make applicable the provisions of the Bill which we look upon as the safeguards. He hias to be there to give a certificate, or to give a certificate of refusal, consequently, we have an enumerator for each poll.

I am only pointing out
that when the Secretary of State instances the conditions in the West as a reason for the provisions of the Bill in the East, the reason is not adequate.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
There is a lot of force
in what my hon. friend from Edmonton says. The provisions as to enumerators are not as applicable to thickly settled districts and large cities as they are to less thickly settled districts. That is one of the reasons why this Act only puts Alberta and Saskatchewan on the same plane as British Columbia and Manitoba. There is no great difference in conditions between British Columbia and Alberta, and there is no great difference between Manitoba and Saskatchewan. When we come to the eastern provinces, however, where the population is more dense, and where theie are larger cities, then we adopt the provincial lists that are here, and in the larger cities we provide for revision before we go to the poll, that is to say, we only partially adopt the enumeration system in those eastern provinces. Indeed, we only adopt it for the purposes of putting on the women who are now entitled and taking off the aliens who are disentitled.

When I spoke the other day I suggested to the Government the desirability of making provision for registration in the cities of Saskatchewan. I confined it to my own province, but I have no doubt that it would be applicable to Alberta as well. In the city of Saskatoon, or Regina, or Moosejaw, or Prince Albert, there are many people moving about, commercial travellers and others, and it would be very difficult to pursue the system which is outlined in this Bill where votes may be challenged on election day, where the right of the voter to vote becomes the subject of investigation and where it will be necessary for the voter to hang around in continual readiness to prove his right to vote. On that account I suggest to the minister that it would be desirable to have registration under officers appointed by himself. Appeals can be taken and the lists will be completed in plenty of time before the election. I hope he will give that consideration.

We are wandering over several clauses of this Bill, and I d.o not think we can make progress or discuss it in any intelligible way unless we take it up paragraph by paragraph. I suggest we take it up paragraph by paragraph and stick to it.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: We are at paragraph 32.

Upon this paragraph, 32,
I would like to know if the Government cannot see their way clear, as the Secretary of State told us yesterday that this Bill was for the purpose of enlarging the scope of the franchise, to enlarge it a little further. The right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert .Borden) yesterday, in referring to the difficulty of extending the franchise to women generally spoke of matters of naturalization and some other things which should not stand in the way. There are things that could be easily obviated, by designation as we do designate in paragraph 33 (a) certain things with regard to women relatives of men in the overseas force or who have been overseas. I would like to know if the Government have given this consideration and whether they are prepared to shut out from the franchise, in view of the recognition of the female relatives of men who are serving overseas, all the women in this country, say, of British birth and British origin, who have given all they were able to give, their time, their energy and their ability to war work. Surely a difficulty as to the naturalization might very fairly be overcome by designation. I would like to know if the Government will not consider enlarging the franchise in this regard.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
This subject comes under paragraph 33 (a) rather than 32 but I might as well give my answer now as we have virtually passed 32. Thirty-two is really a clause of the old Act any way.
With reference to 33 (a), the Government has given very long, careful, if not prayerful thought to the subject that the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) has brought to our attention. The difficulty in regard to naturalization is only one of the difficulties in the way. I noted with very great interest that, while the hon. member for Humboldt thought it could be got over by designation, he did not suggest any designation of those who should be included

and of those who should be left out. That was our difficulty too. If all were included that difficulty of naturalization would be insuperable.
I did say British by birth.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The hon. 'member means to include all who are British by birth?
And Canadian.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Then about three-fourths of the argument of yesterday directed against this whole question of discrimination would be levelled against us if we adopted that because that is discriminating against those who are British subjects now and have not the franchise while all the rest get it. The speech of the leader of the Opposition would Teach us with direct force if we adopted that course., With naturalization on its present basis-and it cannot be altered very well now without an Imperial understanding-it is not just and right that those others naturalized should
4 p.m. be in a Jbetter position than those who are naturalized by personal application. That is one of our difficulties. The other difficulty which most distinctly applies to the suggestion of the hon. member for Humboldt that all other women of British birth be included is that if all of British birth are included then this franchise extended to the female relatives of soldiers loses its representative value altogether. It is nothing to the soldier if 'all women described in that way are included. It is making no' quid pro quo to him because he in part loses his franchise and wholly loses his influence. Of the soldiers who have gome to the front 26,000 are dead 'and several thousand are prisoners of war. That is giving him nothing in lieu of what should be made up to him in a war-time election. Once you go as far as my hon. friend suggests, then the women's franchise loses its representative character and value altogether and the main necessity for the Bill is wiped away. I know of no way else to draw the line which will at the same time meet the difficulty as to naturalization, and, on the other hand, and moie important in my estimation, make the women's vote representative of the soldiers overseas.

I appreciate the point of the Solicitor General in desiring to make up during the next election for the loss of the influence which those overseas would have if they were here by giving their relatives the franchise which, to some extent, 
might compensate 'them for that. While this has been mentioned before, it is put forward so prominently now by the minister that it strikes me that this feature is not a feature in the enfranchisement of women. It is doubling the franchise of men. It is not put forward as a measure of suffrage to women because they are women. It is multiplying the influence of men and it is put forward on that ground.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Not multiplying-just
keeping up the regular standard.
Air. AleCRANEY: It is very irregular, because the female vote may be from one to half a dozen in case of some soldiers. I am not complaining about it. I am only showing the character of it. Perhaps it is not always possible to be consistent. The Government does not profess to be consistent on all occasions, and I do not know why members on this side of the House should be expected to be. I would not ask the Government, in the view which they hold, to extend the franchise to the women of the country on the same terms as it is extended to men. My chief objection to this Bill is the fact that some will be disfranchised, who now have a vote. Perhaps we would not enfranchise some of them, if we were starting de novo. But I feel that there is a great body of earnest women in this country whose sentiments are loyal, and who are showing those sentiments by the work they are doing. If the suggestion of my hon. friend from Humboldt (Mr. Neely) has made, that women who are British subjects be enfranchised were adopted, it would go a long way. It would not enfranchise those womep who have become British subjects by operation of law, and, perhaps, in declining to enfranchise them my hon. friend has in mind the wives of the men whom he proposes to disfranchise, and probably he objects to their becoming enfranchised.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I want the hon. gentleman to understand that the wives, sisters, daughters, and mothers of that class who may be overseas are enfranchised by this Bill, just the same as any other.
Mr. AleCRANEY: But the Prime Alin-ister's statement is that that class are not accepted as recruits, and if they become soldiers they must represent themselves as Russians, or some other nationality.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Aly hon. friend does not draw one distinction which he ought to dTaw. I was not speaking of wo-

men of any nationality. In the observations which I made yesterday in regard to naturalization I was speaking of women who were not British subjects by birth.

I quite understand the statement of the Prime Minister in reference to that, but I am assuming-and no doubt the minister will correct me if I am wrong-that the reason women who are naturalized by operation of law, through the fact' of their husbands being naturalized, are not included in the franchise, is because the Government realized that it would enfranchise that large body of women who are wives of the foreign clajS which they propose to disfranchise.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: This Bill affects the alien enemy foreigner, but to enfranchise women generally would enfranchise the wives, sisters and all the other relatives of men born in other countries, not alien enemy at all, not speaking the alien enemy language, but speaking Norwegian or Russian, and people from all the countries of the world. It deals with a very much wider class.

If the measure enfranchised the wives of all British-born subjects, I would be satisfied if it enfranchised, in addition to those, the wives of all who came from other than alien enemy countries. It strikes me the reason the Government is confining the franchise as it does is because it fears to enfranchise the wives of the men whom they are disfranchising.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Well, in part. But the hon. gentleman will follow me in two small steps of reasoning: in the first place, had we taken that course, and enfranchised the British born, and the British born alone, then the argument advanced by the leader of the Opposition, that persons resident in Canada, naturalized-and consequently given this pact as he describes it, if it is a pact-are discriminated against, would come with crushing force on us. That is the argument the hon. gentleman is advancing now. He could not endorse the position taken by the hon. leader of the Opposition yesterday, and stand where he is to-day. The second point-and in my judgment a much more important point- is that to enfranchise all the British-born women of Canada would be no remuneration to the soldiers overseas for what they are denied by virtue of a war election. There would be no compensation for them in that, and the Bill would lose its main
purpose, and, indeed, its main justification.
1 think the hon. member for Saskatoon will see that this is impracticable. How can we go through an election, and say to those overseas:	" Those who stay at
home can use their influence, canvass, go from door to door, make their appeals, and all the weaker passions of our nature can be played upon by the demagogue and i everyone else, but you men overseas, who have other motives and principles, cannot do so, and we will hold an election while you are 4,000 miles away, and deny you the right to exercise any personal influence whatever, and will also deny you 50 per cent of your vote." That is the condition we are endeavouring to repair. But if you give all the British-born a vote, you do not repair that condition in any sense at all. In peace times, it would be justified, but if you give it now, you deny to the soldiers overseas that influence which it is the purpose of this Bill to give.

My hon. friend is emphasizing that point very much. I am quite satisfied that if the women of the city in which I live who are British subjects by birth were enfranchised, they would support the soldiers at the front.
Hear, hear.

The Solicitor General is assuming that they would be antagonistic. I am putting forward this argument, because day after day the women are going to the Red Cross room, and carrying on such activities, and I would like, without laying myself open to charges of inconsistency, to try and work out something practicable, so that these women, other than those entitled to vote because of ties of relationship, shall have some say, and shall be able to exercise their influence in the same direction as those who have ties with the soldier.

I do not think the Solicitor General puts the ground for giving the right of voting to the relatives of the soldiers upon the right basis. I do not think it is intended to give to the relatives of the soldiers the right to vote in order that they may represent the soldiers, but the vote is to be given to the women because of the sacrifices they have made, by reason of their relationship.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Both reasons.

It seems to me the
latter is the true reason-that they have made the very greatest sacrifice a woman

can make in parting with those dear to them; I think that it is the true ground upon which the argument should be based. If I were a soldier I would rather trust the ordinary women of the country than my own relatives to see that I was treated fairly in everything. The ordinary women of the country would not be interested especially through ties of blood; they would be interested as citizens, as women of Canada; and I am satisfied that they could be relied upon to see that absolute justice was done to soldiers in the matter of their support at the front and of proper provision for them on their return. In the matter of allowances to their relatives, in the matter of separation allowance, in t'he matter of pensions, do you not think that the ordinary woman would be even more generous in her demands than the relative of the soldier would be? It seems to me that the Secretary of State does not present any argument against the extension of the franchise to those persons whom the member for Montreal, St. Lawrence, Mr. Bicker-dike) called the loyal and patriotic women of Canada.
The Prime Minister makes objection to extending the franchise to women generally on the ground that conditions affecting the naturalization laws have to be considered. Surely that difficulty, if it is a difficulty, must have presented itself to the Prime Minister two- or three months ago when he assured the women's delegations who waited upon 'him that the franchise would -be extended generally to the women of the country. On the 16th of May last, the following resolution was moved by the member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland):
That, In the opinion of this House, the question of extending- the franchise Ito women should engage the attention of the Government at the present session.
That resolution was received sympathetically by the Prime Minister; he gave the women of the country to understand that the Government would act upon it. During the course of the discussion I moved the following amendment:
That all the words after the word "That" be struck out and tlje following substituted therefor:	.
"the Dominion Election Act should be so-amended at the present session as to make uniform the right of women to vote for members of the House of Commons in those provinces which have granted to them -the provincial franchise."
That (amendment was ruled out of order by t'he Speaker. He said:
The member has on the Order Paper a resolution No. 6, following this one, which it seems 
to -me, although it is not in the same terms, is substantially the same as the one which he now submits by way of amendment. Bourinot says, page 301, [DOT]'Nor is it regular to move as an amendment to a question a motion of which notice has been given and which appears in its place on the notice paper."
The question being again proposed on the amendment, the Prime Minister moved the following amendment to the motion of the member for South Oxford:
That all the words after the word "That" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this House the question of extending the franchise to women should engage the attention of Parliament -before an appeal to the people is made."
And the question being proposed on the 'amendment, I moved an amendment to the amendment in the following words:
That the following words be added thereto: "and it is therefore desirable that a measure having this object in view should be submitted to Parliament by the Government during the present session."
A debate arose upon that, and on the motion of the member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) the debate was adjourned. On a number of occasions since then I have been (assured by gentlemen- leading the H-ouse [DOT]that an opportunity would be given for the discussion of this motion, of the amendment -moved by the Prime Minister -and of the amendment to the -amendment moved by myiself. Bat the -important thing is that my right hon. friend moved as an amendment that the matter of extending the franchise to women should engage the (attention of Parliament before -an appeal to the people was made. That w-a-s an assurance to the House and to the wo-men of the country that the Government wa-s favourable to -extending ithe franchise generally to the women of Canada. There is no doubt -about that; the women of Canada so understood it; they expressed themselves as thankful to the Government for having at last decided to ask Parliament to grant them equal rights of suffrage. My right hon. friend put forth objections of a fanciful character as an explanation why the right of suffrage is granted to a few-I admit that it -should be granted to them; they have strong claims to it-and is refused to hundreds of thousands of other women who are equally entitled to it. No harm can come from extending the franchise generally to the women of Canada;
I am satisfied that every possible good would come from it. The Government ought not to let this session pass, it ought not allow this Bill to be disposed of, with-

out making provision for extending the franchise to women generally. If there are any objections on the ground of nationality or naturalization, then let the franchise be limited to the British-born women of Canada. That would extend the franchise to several hundred thousand women who, as I said yesterday, have shown during this war, by the unceasing work which they have done and the splendid patriotism which they have evidenced, that they are as capable of exercising the franchise as the men. They have shown that they are just as much concerned in the good government of this country and in the welfare of this Dominion as the men who exercise the franchise to-day. I was much struck by the remark of a lady who was very much in favour of suffrage and who spoke many times on the subject in the western provinces. Somebody suggested that the women might make a mess of politics. Well, she said, a much worse mess could not be madp of it than is being made to-day; the women could not do very much worse than the men. That is true. The men do it as well as they can, but I am satisfied that the women, if they were given the right to vote, would in many cases do very much better than the men. No good reason can be urged against giving the women the right of the franchise. I appeal to the hon. gentleman who introduced the resolution to which I have referred to repeat the arguments which he presented on that occasion. The women of this country are waiting to receive a message that the Government will carry out their pledge. My right hon. friend says that some of the women, recognizing that the Government have gone quite a distance, believe that the Government ought to receive the thanks of the women. That may be so, but these women have been, deceived; they have been led to believe that this is simply a War-time Elections Act, the effect of which will end when the war is over. That is not true. It is nowhere provided by legislation that there is to be a new general election when this war is over. But the men, whether they will be Liberals or Conservatives, who will be elected under this proposed franchise, will be the representatives of the people and will have charge of the administration of affairs for the next five years, Supposing this war should end in a year, they will be in charge for four years after it is over. I am satisfied that, when the women of this country realize that they are to be debarred from the exercise of the franchise, of having any control over the affairs of this country during the next
five years, my right hon. friend will hear from them in very loud tones. I am told that even to-day my right hon. friend has been requested to receive delegations in order to hear their representations. I have been given this telegram from Vancouver, dated the 8th of September:
Have wired Premier following United Suffrage Societies' protest against Election Act now before House re woman suffrage which disfranchises women of British Columbia. Object to any extension of franchises to women except on same terms as to men. Demand federal franchise for women who are qualified as men are qualified.
(Sgd.) United Suffrage Societies.
I am told that is a very large, representative, influential organization, having its headquarters in Vancouver, and I am satisfied they represent the feeling of the women throughout this country. They have been demanding the franchise; they have been led to expect that they will receive the franchise, and as I have said, at last they thought they had the absolute promise of my right hon. friend that the franchise would be given to them. The attitude of my right hon. friend at first-some two or three years ago when, a delegation of women waited upon him, was that it was a matter for the provincial legislatures to deal with. He led the women, of this country to believe that whenever the provincial legisla-ures extended to women the Tight of suffrage, ipso facto, they would have the right to vote for members of this Parliament. Five provinces of Canada have given to women the right of suffrage. Under the assurance that was then given by the Prime Minister, they had a right to suppose that, at all events as to those provinces, the right of suffrage in voting for members for this Parliament would be extended to them. When the matter came up in the House, the Prime Minister hesitated to ask Parliament to enact Legislation which would carry out that view. I remember, either one or two sessions ago, when I introduced a resolution expressly providing for that, feeling sure that I would have the hearty support of the Prime Minister, he called upon his supporters to vote down the resolution, and, in consequence, it was defeated. During this session, my right hon. friend has led the women of this country to believe-at least so I am informed, because I was not present at the meeting, but the matter was reported in the press-that a general right of suffrage would be granted to them. Certainly, his attitude in this House when he
COMMONS moved the amendment to the resolution of the hon. member for South Oxford (Mt. Sutherland) that the question of extending the franchise to the women should engage the attention of Parliament before dissolution, was one that was calculated to lead Parliament and the people of the country to believe that a general measure of franchise would be submitted to Parliament at the present session.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend apparently forgets that, when he proposed a motion at the present session-the motion to which he has just now alluded-he phrased it in this way:
In the opinion of this House it is desirable that provision be made either to grant to women who are qualified to vote for members of a Provincial Legislature, the right also to vote for members of the Dominion Parliament, or to grant to women throughout the Dominion the right to vote for members of Parliament, subject to such provisions and limitations as may seem reasonable to Parliament.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The proposal
of my hon. friend in the first instance, made one or two sessions ago, was that we should enact in this Parliament legislation making it possible for women who had the right of provincial franchise to exercise that right of franchise in federal elections. A good deal has been said about discrimination. I imagine that the women of Canada, in the provinces in which they have not hitherto received the franchise in provincial elections, would look upon that as a very grave discrimination, if the Government should carry it out. But I pointed out also to my hon. friend-although he speaks lightly of the question of haturalization to which I alluded yesterday-that, in the tends of the motion I have just read, he himself recognized the importance of certain provisions and limitations which might seem reasonable to Parliament. I do not wish to repeat what I said yesterday on this point. I endeavoured to make myself perfectly clear, and I hope I did so. My hon. friend now suggests-along the principle of his motion of two years ago, but entirely in opposition to the view put forward by his leader yesterday-that we should amend the provisions of this Bill by providing that women of British birth should have the franchise and- that women torn in other countries, who were not of British nationality, should not have that right. The leader of the Opposition urged, with all the force at his command, that the provisions of this measure

would prevent people from coming to this country as immigrants. W'hat my hon. friend is urging just now would be a very much wider example of discrimination. Women who came to this country from the United Staes of America, or who came from France and other Allied nations, would be discriminated against by the proposal of my hon. friend. The observations of the leader of the Opposition would have very much greater force if directed against the hon. member for St. John than they had when directed against the proposal embodied in this Bill.
I realize at once that there are .in this country many women who, under the provisions of this Bill, will not have the vote at the coming election. I realize fully also, that at least a great majority of the women have worked untiringly and devotedly in aid of the purpose of Canada in this war. So far as these observations of my hon. friend are concerned, I entirely fconcur in the appreciation he has expressed. But we have to deal with conditions as they are in this country to-day. We have to deal with the situation which I described in my remarks of yesterday. I adhere entirely to the opinion that I have already expressed more than once in this House, namely, that the women of Canada generally are entitled to the franchise, and if the people of this country should give to me a mandate at the next general election, 1 undertake to carry out the purpose that I have already proclaimed. I propose to carry that out according to those lines and subject to the observations which I made on this point yesterday. Therefore, so far as that general principle is concerned, there will be no departure from it so far as my action may control it. But we are dealing now with an election in time of war. We are dealing with this question at a time , when the life of Parliament will expire in less than four weeks. We are dealing with it under conditions of an unusual character in many ways. When we come to consider the question of naturalization, we have to take into account that it has been the purpose of the statesmen of all the selfgoverning nations of the British Empire to have one uniform system of naturalization, and that the naturalization so established shall be effective throughout the Empire and not, as previously established, effective only in the Dominion or in the nation where the naturalization was granted. So when we come to look at it in the aspect which commends itself to my mind, wq find ourselves confronted with this situa-

tion: The women of this country,, if they are entitled to the franchise, are entitled also to determine their citizenship. I do not think any hon. gentleman in this House or any man or woman in this country would gainsay that. If a woman is entitled to her full voice in the affairs of this country, then that woman is entitled to determine her citizenship for herself, and not to have it determined for her by the mere fact of her marriage. But in order to bring that about, and to remove the anomalies which the present system creates, it will be necessary to pass legislation which will have to be very carefully considered, and as to which there ought to be negotiations with the Mother Country and with the other self-governing dominions of the Empire if we are to preserve the uniformity which at the conference of 1911 was regarded as essential, and if we are to preserve one type and form of naturalization for the whole British Empire. I am sure every one in this icountry will realize the absolute impossibility of accomplishing all that between now and the 7th of October, when the life of this Parliament expires.
My hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) reproaches me because he considers I have not given sufficient attention to the subject during the past six or seven weeks. I would point out to him that we have had half a dozen matters engaging the attention of the Government during this season, any one of which under ordinary conditions would have been regarded as a sufficient undertaking for a government during one whole session of Parliament. We have had to grapple with these questions as best we could, and it may be possible that owing to those circumstances, and not to any indisposition on my part, adequate attention has not been given to the particular feature which I brought to the notice of the House yesterday. That has been our misfortune, and not our fault. At all events, we are dealing with conditions as they are now, and I say once more: it would be impossible for this Parliament in the limited time which will elapse between now 'and the 7th of October to give to that question the consideration and the attention which "it deserves, .and, more than that, to have the communication with the Government and Parliament of the Mother Country and of itihe Overseas Dominions which would be necessary if we are to preserve the essential feature of uniformity in naturalization throughout the Empire which was laid down as a guiding principle at the conference of 1911, and
which was carried out so far as the Mother Country and some of the Dominions iare concerned, by the legislation enacted in 1914.
I realize fully that there may be women in tins country-there doubtless are-who will not be entitled to the franchise under this Bill .and who may feel aggrieved about it. But I am .also convinced that when they come to realize and comprehend the situation which confronts the Government at this time, .they will give the Government credit for dealing with the question in a fair and reasonable way, and for doing what they could to give the franchise to a very large body of Canadian womanhood- and this Bill will undoubtedly grant the franchise to a very large number of the women of this country. I know that there are those who have worked unceasingly and devotedly who have not immediate relatives *at the front, but who are as earnest in their purpose and1 in .their endeavour as any woman in Canada could be. I hope and believe they will understand and comprehend this situation.
As far as we are concerned, I repeat onct more that we have endeavoured to frame this Bill on the guiding principle of service and of sacrifice. While I give every credit that could be given to those devoted women in Canada who have not relatives at the front, but who nevertheless have thrown their whole heart and soul into the national purpose, yet it must be conceded, even by these women themselves, that those women have made the greater sacrifice who have sent to the front those who are nearest p.nd dearest to them to fight for our institutions, for our liberties, and for the preservation of this Empire.

We all recognize that in giving this Bill its second reading Parliament was recognizing the principle of discrimination so far as the franchise is concerned. The Government recognized that the Bill was open to criticism from the fact that m extending the franchise to women they had to draw a line somewhere. The Prime Minister had just admitted that injury may be done to many of the women of Canada who have given splendid service since the outbreak of the war, and who will not be enfranchised by this Bill. I presume that in the matter of disfranchising the electors the same holds good, and that the Government are not satisfied with the cfegree of disfranchisement this Bill proposes. They would go further if they could, or it' they dared; but they have gone as far

I do not know about that. Is there not an insinuation in the position taken by the Secretary of State that the only women in this country who can be trusted to multiply or increase the influence of the soldier overseas in an election are his own immediate relatives. I think this Bill puts an imputation, on a percentage of the women of this country, which is absolutely unworthy of this- Parliament. While I know that the eliminating effect of this Bill, so far as the franchise is concerned, dees not go as far as the Government would like, is there any justification or any reason why in provinces where women's fran-
chise has already been adopted, and the principle is accepted, where *we are by this very Bill trusting the men to vote, we should not also trust -these men's wives? I quite understand that the proposal of the Government is to disfranchise certain of our male electors, and presumably they will not trust the wives or daughters of these male electors, at this forthcoming election, hut is there any reason why in those provinces where women's franchise has already been granted, the wives and daughters of electors who have not been disfranchised should not have the right to vote? That is standing by the underlying principle of the present Dominion franchise, namely, that in so far as possible we adopt the provincial standard of qualification, and it is the Government's intention and hope, they would have us believe, that they are trying to depart from that principle just as little as possible in the present Bill. That obviates all the difficulties the Prime Minister was speaking about. Stick by the provincial franchise and provincial standard of qualification, except in so far as the Government is determined to disfranchise a certain class of the electors. That, of course, we presume will naturally tell against the wives and the daughters of those electors as well as against -the men themselves. I think it is a sound principle to adopt the provincial franchise, and as far as we adopt the provincial franchise if we trust the male elector to retain his franchise, we should also trust his wife and daughter.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman intimates something -about my not trusting any woman except those who have sons overseas. That is not the point at all. If is not a question of trusting the women- of Canada to stand by the war. There -are differences of opinion as to how practically to stand by o-ur boys and by the war, and in the judgment o-f the Government those who would most likely share the opinions of the men overseas as to the best -method and the only method of doing so would be their near relatives. It is not unreasonable to presume that the sentiments of the overseas force would be best reflected by Canada in their own immediate relatives. I do not think that is illogical or unreasonable. That is as far as I have gone, and that is as far as I need go to justify the measure. The amendment moved by my bon. friend looks to the adoption throughout Canada of the provincial franchise. If it is passed, then wherever or whosoever she -be, a woman

who can vote in any province can vote in the Dominion elections. Let us get the full meaning of this, so that the House may understand it, and with this in view, I think it is just as well that the amendment has been moved. In the four western provinces all naturalized British subjects, no matter how they are naturalized, get the vote. If a woman comes from Germany, or Austria, *and marries three weeks after she arrives, she becomes naturalized, and is entitled to the vote.
Not according to the other provisions.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Not according to the
other provisions, because they are in direct conflict with this. The other provisions are in accord with section 32 as it stands, but you cannot change paragraph 32 if the other provision stands. The contention of the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) is that we shall adopt the provincial franchise as to women. Let hon. gentlemen understand what the effect of that would be. If a woman who has been a week in Canada marries a naturalized citizen, she thereby becomes a naturalized British subject. That is the law of the land to-day.

She would not he entitled
to vote,

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: She would be entitled to vote immediately she had the residence required by the province.

Does not the minister see that by this paragraph the qualifications necessary to enable any male or female person to vote at a Dominion election in any province shall, except as by this Act otherwise provided, be those established by the law's of that province. Could it not be easily worked out in some other sections?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: If this passes who would be able to vote, and who would not?

If my hon. friend thinks it desirable to disqualify men of alien enemy origin, I presume he would also disqualify the wives of men of alien enemy origin. That could be easily done because if the majority of the House determines that those men should be disfranchised, naturally their wives would also be disfranchised.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I would like to get the intention of the hon. member for Humboldt. Is it his intention by the amendment that there would be disfranchisement of the wives of Germans, Austrians, Turks, and
Bu'garians, naturalized within the last fifteen years?

Most assuredly. I said
we should recognize the principle of discrimination; you would have to do so.
'Mr. MEIGHEN: That would not be the effect of the amendment if it passed although of course, other clauses could be changed accordingly to bring about that effect. In so far as the alien enemy born are concerned, any one of them naturalized within the last fifteen years would not be able to vote, whether male or female, but in so far as Swedish bom are concerned, a woman would be a naturalized British subject the moment she landed in Canada if she then married, and as soon she acquired her residence in the province, whatever it might be-it is one year-she would be entitled to vote. Is it the intention of the hon. member for Humboldt that the man should be required to be here three or five years, before he could become a naturalized citizen and have the right to vote, and that the woman could get that right in one year?

She will only have the right to vote and come under the operation of the franchise if she marries a British subject. So far as I am personally concerned, I would say in answer to the Secretary of State, .that I would be perfectly willing to trust with the franchise a Swedish woman married to a British subject for one year, in war time or any other time.
Mr. MEIGiHEN:	A naturalized British
subject?
Yes.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
That would make her
a British subject. Of course, if she was born in Germany, she would have to be here three years and the man would have to be here five years, but a Swedish woman who marries a naturalized British subject of German origin, after one year's residence, is entitled to a vote. Would the hon. gentleman support that legislation?
That is a side issue. Cases of that kind would be exceedingly few.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There are thousands of them-.

As we are discriminating
we can very easily provide for cases where women marry British subjects of alien enemy birth. If you are taking the franchise away from a man of alien enemy birth it is a simple thing to say that his wife shall not have it.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: If she marries a British subject of alien enemy birth, she will not be entitled to the franchise?
She will not.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: If she marries a British subject who was not of alien enemy birth she will?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Is not that discriminating against a British subject of alien enemy birth? Is that not exactly-what we were warned against yesterday by the hon. gentleman's leaders?

I am not trying to bo consistent because I recognize that the whole Bill is^ q ipass of inconsistencies. We are recognizing the principle of discrimination all through this Bill. We are passing this special Act to get away from the usual Dominion Franchise Act and to do that by a process of discrimination. My point is this:	Keeping, as we hope to do, as near
to the provincial franchise as .possible, where a man has a vote his wife should have a vote also.

The Secretary of State has given as an illustration the case of a Swedish woman who came hare and married a naturalized British subject who, under this Act, would have had to be here since 1902. We take it for granted that he would be a proper British subject if he had been here during that time. I would be .perfectly willing to give that woman a vote. I have no dread of that sort of a voter. I have no such dread of the naturalized 5 p.m. alien as my hon. friend has. [DOT]

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Why not give the same right to the man?
Why not? I cannot see why not.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
If a woman was a
naturalized British subject. and a Swede came to Canada and .married her next day would my hon. friend be prepared to give that 2n.an a vote?

If the Swede were here
a year and if he had become a British subject I would give him a vote.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: A naturalized German woman who has been here since 1902 is entitled to a vote. A Swedish man comes here and marries her the next day after he arrives. Would the hon. gentleman give that man a vote?
No, not the next day.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
That is what he wants to give the woman.
Mr. hESBITT:	He would have to wait
a year.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: He would have to wait a year by the law of the province but lie would be a British subject next day after his arrival. My hon. friend would give him a vote after a year's residence in Canada?

Sure I would. I do not object to giving these men votes. There are lots of men up in my constituency who will be disqualified and who are just as loyal and just as good citizens as the Secretary of State is.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I only want to know
what the hon. gentleman intends. If he intends that, all right.	,

Sure; that is what I intend. I would not cut them out. My hon. friend here (Mr. Neely) has moved a resolution which I am going to second and which follows the provincial law. The provincial Act does not say that if they are here a month or a day they shall be naturalized as British subjects. My hon. friend knows that.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes, they can become British subjects in a day.
No.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
They would not have
a vote in a day but they would be naturalized.

What .is the use of splitting hairs in that way? The hon. gentleman, the House, and the country know what I mean. I am not a bit alarmed about these aliens. I have aliens in my constituency, many of whom are serving in the war, who are just as loyal as the Secretary of State is or any gentleman on the other side of the House.
We have in that riding a respectable body of Indians, several of whom have enlisted and have gone overseas. Will the squaws in that case have a right to vote?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Not under the Bill as it stands, fox this reason, that the Bill requires women to qualify as to age, race, and residence in accordance with the laws of the provinces, iand under the laws of the provinces the Indian race has not a vote.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My hon. friend the Secretary of State yesterday took credit

for having granted the franchise to a new class of voters, to the women who are relatives in near degree of the men who have enlisted. So far so good; nobody quarrels with that. But my hon. friend, while actuated 'by this praiseworthy motive, cannot conceal the fact that he is taking away the franchise from many female subjects of His Majesty who ought to have it if the law were properly carried out. I understand that my hon. friend proposes to maintain the principle of the provincial franchise in this Bill; and wants to depart as little as possible from the laws that exist to-day except that he proposes to extend the franchise to the female relatives of the men at the front, and that he is taking it away from voters of alien origin. As the law exists to-day in five provinces, women have the franchise. We had this discussion yesterday, but we are now considering the framing of this measure, and it is perhaps as well that we should have a little more discussion on it. Section 6 of the Dominion Elections Act, which we are now amending, reads:
For the purposes of any Dominion election held within the limits of a province, the voters' Lists shall, except as herein otherwise provided, be those prepared for the several polling divisions established, and which, on the sixtieth day next preceding the day fixed for the nomination of candidates for such Dominion election, were in force, or were last in force, under the laws of that province, for the purposes of provincial elections.
Mark the words with which this section begins: For the purposes of any Dominion election held within the limits of a province, the voters' lists shall, except as herein otherwise provided, be the voters' lists for a Dominion election. My hon. friend told us yesterday what is well known to be a fact, that in Manitoba and British Columbia the ' lists which are now in existence have the names of female voters upon them.
I would think that, if a Dominion election were held under the Act as it stands, these men and women who are on the list in Manitoba and British Columbia would have a right to vote. The Secretary of State shakes his head. Yesterday we were told that the law officers of the Crown, the Minister of Justice, the Solicitor General, and the Deputy Minister of Justice, were of opinion this this Bill did not give the franchise to women. Of course, every man has his own way of interpreting the law.
I may be right in my view, or the interpretation placed upon the Bill by the law offi-' cers of the' Crown may be the correct one, but we have to accept the opinion expressed
by the law officers of the Crown. I should like to have a judicial interpretation, but that is not possible. In my view, the language is as plain as plain can be. I think that the lists have to be taken as they are, and that the provincial franchise in any province is the one upon which the law is to be administered, and under which the Dominion elections are to be held. The minister told us yesterday that section 6 did not apply to women. I do not (understand why it should not apply. If the law of the province makes a person an elector, and that elector has the right to vote in a provincial election, I cannot understand why he should not also have the right to vote at a Dominion election. There is no question in such a case, if it be- a male voter, that he has the right to vote at a Dominion election, but it is said that a female voter has not the same right and I cannot understand why. The law officers of the Crown have decided otherwise, and we must abide by their decision. If the law to-day is that women in the five provinces of Ontario, Saskatchewan, Alberta, Manitoba, and British Columbia have the right to vote at provincial elections, there is one thing certain, namely, that these women expect to have the right to vote at Dominion elections, and they will all claim it. My hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) states that the Premier has been deluged with telegrams from women protesting against being excluded from the operation, of this Bill, and if section 6 of the Dominion Elections Act is not sufficient to caver the point, and grant the right of suffrage to these women who have had it in the five provinces, why should it not be provided that they should have it?
