My hon. friend has Tather played upon words, in his answer to the hon. .member for Humboldt a moment ago. He puts the case of a Swedish woman marrying an alien, and he stated that she would not have the right to vote. That is a very nice point. These women would have to choose between the husband on one side, and suffrage on the other. A woman would have to decide whether she would rather have a husband and no vote, or a vote and no husband. What reason can be urged why these women who have the provincial franchise in these five provinces should not .have the franchise for tlhe Dominion? My hon. friend's Bill reads:
The qualifications necessary to enable any male person to vote at a Dominion election in any province shall, except as in the Act otherwise provided, be those established by, the laws of that province as necessary to entitle such

male person to vote in the same part of the province at a provincial election.
In a subsequent part of the Bill there are provisions to exclude some of the women who to-day are voters in the provinces. Those of .alien, origin who have been naturalized since 31st March, 1902, are excluded. If tihe amendment of my hon. friend from Humboldt were accepted, the Bill would read:
The Iqualiflcations necessary to enable any male or female person to vote at a Dominion election in any province shall, except as by this Act otherwise provided, be those established by the laws of that province as necessary to entitle such male or female person to vote in the same part of the province at a provincial election.
Necessarily, if this provision were accepted, it would have to be qualified later on by the same provision which excludes men of .alien birth from voting. That would follow as a consequence; a certain number of those women might be excluded also, and in the .s*ame way a certain number of men are excluded from the franchise. At all events, the franchise would remain to those women who are not wives of aliens, but the wives of British subjects by birth or otherwise. That cannot be contemplated by the Act, and it seems to me that no good reason has been advanced by the Secretary of State why the amendment of the hon. member for Humboldt should not be accepted. It all comes back to this: Shall women have the franchise or not. My hon. friend has stated, and the Prime Minister repeated, that the only basis for suffrage for women was service and sacrifice. Well, there are different degrees of sacrifice. There is greater service and there is less service. It is a question of degree. But, at all events, nobody can deny that there has been service. It is freely recognized by the Prime Minister, and by the Secretary of State, that all classes of women have been serving. Some have served to the limit of their ability, but all have made more or less sacrifice. Under the circumstances, if the principle is to be adopted it should be followed in all its consequences, especially in these provinces where the women have the provincial franchise, and where it is thought by a majority of the electors that they should be permitted to participate in the rights exercised by men. '

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I draw attention of the leader of the Opposition to the fact that section 6 provides the list, and does not give the franchise. Section 6 says:
 <
For the purpose of any Dominion election held Within the limits of a province the voters' list shall, except as herein otherwise provided ....
What is "otherwise provided''?
Section 10 reads:
The qualifications necessary to entitle any person to vote at a Dominion election in any pi-ovince shall, except as herein otherwise, provided, be those established by the laws of that province as necessary to entitle such person to vote in the same part of the province at a provincial election.
And other sections say that' minors and judges shall not vote. The franchise is provided for in other sections. This section provides how the list of those qualified in that way shall be compiled as the list for the election. The courts havie held, rightly or wrongly, that the word "person'' as used in relating to the franchise, cannot be held to include both sexes, i im not arguing whether the law courts are right or wrong. The law officers of the Crown iiave advised-and I have looked into it as carefully -as I can-that that is the effect of the decision.
Has the question ever come before the courts in Canada?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The question never
came before the courts of Canada, but it has been decided in the courts of England under precisely similar conditions.
It is very different there.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I want to explain the
reason why our point of view was arrived at. I did not rely on my own opinion in the matter. The opinion given by our law officers is very powerfully supported. It is quite true that, if the amendment moved by the hon. member for Humboldt were adopted, by a few changes later oil, the law could be made to adjust itself and have the effect the hon. leader of the Opposition contends for, namely, that of including in the female franchise all those who are in a similar position to those included in the male franchise. But I contend that that would not be a fair effect, for three reasons. First, because of our naturalization laws many women would be enabled to get the franchise after one year's residence in Canada. Second, the representative compensating character and value would be altogether removed from the franchise. A great dead would be done, it is true, in the way of giving the franchise to the women of Canada, but no special compensation would be

given to the soldier. From 'the electoral standpoint, the provision would be of just as much service to the slacker at home as it would be to the soldier overseas; indeed, it would be of more service to the former. Lastly, the change would not follow a clear, bold line of sacrifice. I know that there are other lines of service than that of having a son or a brother at the front; there is very useful service, frequently the best that any woman can give. But you cannot measure that kind of service. We were asiked yesterday to include in the provisions of this Bill those who knitted socks for the soldiers. How many socks? Half a sock, one sock, two socks or a thousand socks? We have to adopt a bold, clear line; we have to take the line that differentiates those who make the highest sacrifice from those who make what must be described as a minor sacrifice.
My horn, friend is seeking to cast ridicule upon the work of the women in making .socks for the soldiers.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Not at all.
Mr. PUGSLEY; The women of this country, as has been admitted, have made every sacrifice it has been possible for them to make in connection with the war. I submit that no argument can be offered against the desirability and justice of giving them the right to vote. I am willing to support the amendment moved by the member for Humbold (Mr. Neely). If nothing more can be done for the women of the country, at least the franchise ought not to be taken away from them in the provinces where they now enjoy it. The Solicitor-General knows that he is taking away the Tight of franchise from some of the women of Canada. He puts in as the qualification for voting the words which are applied to Alberta, Saskatchewan and the Yukon, and he repeals or suspends during the period of the war this section which gives the qualification to women in those other provinces. The qualifications for all the provinces but Alberta, Saskatchewan and the Yukon are the provincial lists, whether they include men or women. Section 10 of the Dominion Elections Act, which is suspended by this measure, reads as follows:
The qualifications necessary to entitle any person to vote at a Dominion election in any province shall, except as herein otherwise provided, be those established by the laws of that province as necessary to entitle such person to vote in the same part of the province at a provincial election.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
That is not what we
suspend.

Why did not my hon.
friend continue that section as the section providing the qualification? He docs not do that; he provides that the qualification set out in, section 32 shall be the quali-i fication throughout the Dominion.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Not at all.

In other words, instead of providing for the smaller portions of Canada-Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Yukon-the same qualification that the Dominion Elections Act provides for the rest of the Dominion, he provides that the qualification in respect to those three districts shall apply to the whole Dominion. He suspends the operation of section 10 and brings into force the operation of section 32. As he knows, section 10 applies to all of Canada, except Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Yukon, 'and section 32 relates only to Saskatchewan and Alberta.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: We do not do that at all.
My hon. friend does, because he suspends the whole of part I.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend has
made a curious mistake.
I have not made a curious mistake.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend has it exactly upside down. We repeal section 32 as it is and we adopt section 10 and put it in this Bill.

My hon. friend is wrong. By section 1 of the Bill it is provided that during the war and until the completion of demobilization after the conclusion of peace, the operation of part 1 of the Dominion Election Act shall be suspended.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
But we take section
10 and put it in; and we repeal section 32.

No, my hon. friend
does not put in section 10.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: We do, but we use the word " male."

Instead of using the
word " person- " as it is used in the whole of the Dominion Elections Act except'that part of it which applies to Alberta, Saskatchewan and the Yukon Territory, my hon. friend puts in the word "male." Notwithstanding the advice of the Justice Department, he is not willing to take the



chance that the word " person " means male person. He inserts the word "male," and thereby limits the franchise to male persons in Canada. Surely that is altering the law with regard to women having the right to vote. I affirm, notwithstanding what the Minister of Justice says, that if a woman, whether married or unmarried, is a person in the eye of the law, .she has the right to vote in every province where her name appears on the provincial lists, except in the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and the Yukon Territory. My hon. friend says that he goes by some judgment of a court in England. Well, that judgment was given a long time ago, in a special case, and at a time when women in England were looked upon not as persons, but as chattels. They were the property of their husbands, to all intents and purposes; when they were married whatever they had in the way of personal property went over to the husband by virtue of the marriage contract. That judgment was delivered at a time when people were imbued with the idea laid down by Blackstone that the English law was very tender in dealing with the married woman when it permitted the husband to beat his wife only to a moderate degree. That was the view held in those days as to the status of woman. But through legislation and the decision of the courts, the status of woman has gradually become enlarged. To-day the law of England and of Canada recognizes her as a person, having civil rights just as a man has, and entitled to be recognized as a person. I believe that all the courts of the country, if the question came up, would recognize " woman " as a " person." But as I have said, the Solicitor General is afraid to rest upon the interpretation which would be given to the word person, and so afraid is he of that, and so desirous is he of making it sure that the women of Ontario. Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia shall not be allowed to vote, that he puts the word "male" before the word "person." My hon. friend says that- he also rests upon the view of the Department of Justice. 1 happen to have before me an opinion which has been expressed by a gentleman who formerly occupied the position of Deputy Minister of Justice in Canada, an eminent lawyer, a gentleman who stands at the very top notch amongst the legal men of Canada, a gentleman of great learning and a very high authority. I refer to Mr. Z. A. Lash, and 
this is his opinion as expressed recently in an address to the University of Toronto: After the Ontario Aot giving votes to women has been finally passed, as the Dominion election law now stands women, whose names are on the Ontario voters' lists, would be entitled to vote at Dominion elections. This affords a remarkable illustration of the interlocking or Dominion and provincial jurisdictions and machinery, all working together smoothly and in accordance with the spirit of the constitution.
How does the hon. member, apart from any court decisions, get over our own Dominion Act as to what constitutes a voter?
In what way?

On page 90 of this book of instructions, we find "Information for electors," which says:
The following is the qualification of electors as prescribed by the Parliament of Canada: Every male person shall be qualified to vote at the election of a member under this Act.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What section is that?
It is in one of the schedules arising out of the Act.
I will tell my hon. friend hc.w I shall get over it. My hon. friend happens to be reading the instructions to the electors of Saskatchewan and Alberta.
One further question. Mr. PUGSLEY: That is the answer to tins first.

On page 97 there appear the oaths to be taken by electors. The first oath is:
You do swear that you are of the male sex and a British subject.
If my hon. friend will read the oath carefully, he will find that those are the instructions to and the oath to be taken by the electors in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta and in the Yukon-
Oh, no.

-and only in those provinces and in that territory. Let me show my hon. friend that I am right. This is very important, and I am glad my hon. friend called attention to it. If my hon. friend will look at section 35, which starts with the words-
In the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta.
-he will find that it refers to the proclamation in Form G. Section 32 of this Bill. It says:

In the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, except as in this Act otherwise provided, every male person shall be qualified to vote at the election of a member under this Act, who, not being: an Indian, is a British subject and of the full age of twenty-one years, and has resided in either of the said provinces for at least twelve months.
I am sure my hon. friend will find that the information to which he has referred is the information relating entirely to the voters of Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Yukon Territory.

How about the oath?
Are you going to make a woman swear that she is a man?

I am answering one
thing at a time. We shall now come to the oath. The oath, which my hon. friend dwells upon and which is to be found upon page 97, says:
You do swear that you are of the male sex and a British subject, that you are not an Indian, that you are of the full age of twenty-one years, and that you have resided in the province of Saskatchewan or Alberta or the Yukon Territory (as the case may be) for at least twelve months.

All right.
Mr. PtJGSLEY:	If my hon. friend will
turn to section 61 he will find that that form is the form provided specifically for Saskatchewan, Alberta, and the Yukon Territory.

The electors must be
males.

Section 61 says:
Every deputy returning officer in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta and the Yukon Territory may, and shall, when he is required so to do by any candidate or agent of a candidate, administer to any elector either one or both of the oaths set forth in Form Z.
That is the form to which my hon. friend has referred and which I have just read, and the form which is limited expressly to Saskatchewan, and to Alberta, and to the Yukon Territory.
It deals with male persons, not with female persons, There is nothing about females there.
Of course, it deals with male persons, because part II, relating to Saskatchewan, Alberta, and the Yukon Territory, expressly limits the franchise to male persons.
May I ask my hon. friend a question?
Just wait one minute.
My hon. friend might explain why all the French Canadian members except one have left the Chamber, and that one i6 now leaving.

I suppose they have a perfect right to leave, and I am gratified my hon. friends have remained while I am ad>-addressing the committee. I have a good attendance before me and I have not felt the loss of my French Canadian friends. I will refer to section 153. I feel my hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Morphy) is entitled to have an answer to his question, because he does not suggest ridiculous things in this House.
Take your time.

Section 153 says:
Except in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta and the Yukon Territory, an elector, if required by the deputy returning officer, the poll clerk, one of the candidates, or an agent of a candidate, or by any elector present, shall, before receiving his ballot paper, take such oath of qualification as by the laws of the province he may in the like case at a provincial election be required to take, such changes having been made in the form of oath as are necessary to make it applicable to the election being held, and there being added to such oaths, or substituted therein for any clauses dealing with the like matters or any of them, the clauses set forth in Form Y.
Let us see if Form Y, which is on page 97, says anything about being a male voter. Form Y says:
You swear (or solemnly affirm),-
That you have not been disfranchised under the provisions of the Disfranchising- Act, or for corrupt practices under the Dominion, Elections Act;
That you have not voted before at this election, either at this or at any other polling station ;
That you have not received anything, .	.	.
That you have not, directly or indirectly, paid or promised anything to any person either to induce him to vote or to refrain from voting at this election.
There is no oath or affirmation there that the voter is a male person.
This only gives the corrupt practices part of it. It does not make the voter swear that he is a British subject.

Can my hon. friend
show me where in the Dominion Elections Act the voter is required to swear that he is a male person except in Saskatchewan, Alberta, and the Yukon Territory?
I have not searched for that.

Well, I have. I did so when I moved a resolution in this House

two sessions ago. My hon. friend can [DOT] search the Dominion! Elections Act from beginning to end and examine all the forms, and nowhere will he find the requirement that the voter shall be a male person. The requirements of the statute, and the forms, proclamations and oaths which relate to male persons are limited entirely to those provisions relating to the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta and the Yukon Territory. I can assure my hon. friend that he has only to look at the statute to see that I am absolutely right. But the Secretary of State in this Bill is taking away the right of the women to' vote; at all events the right of the women of the provinces of Ontario, Manitoba and British* Columbia, where if they are persons they have the right to vote. My hon. friend may say they are not persons, but I say they are; a woman has always been recognized as a person in reality and in law, though law sometimes differs from reality. The women of Alberta and Saskatchewan are also on the provincial lists, and this Bill takes away the right which those women have by law to-day to cast their ballots at an election for the Dominion Parliament. My hon. friend has made it clear he is doing that, because he has put in the words "male person" and has made it applicable to the whole of Canada. Therefore, no matter what franchise may be given by any provincial legislature in Canada, when this Bill goes into force, notwithstanding any provincial franchise giving women the right to vote, their names will be struck off the provincial lists. That is wrong, and therefore I am prepared to vote, and vote heartily, for the amendment of my hon. friend from Humboldt.

The question whether the amendment 'Should carry is one of especial interest to a province like my own, where the (franchise has been extended to our women citizens. I am a supporter of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Humboldt, believing that it is an improvement on (the legislation which, the Government has brought down. I am not quarrelling with the legislation which the Government proposes on this particular feature, but I submit that the Government should give more consideration to the possibility that their legislation can be improved upon. It is unfortunate that the Government seems to take the position that because ia suggestion comes from this side of the House it must be laughed out of court, or met with taunt, or sophistry, or something 
like that. The leader of the Government gets up and says that on a certain occasion the leader of the Opposition, or the hon. member for St. John, said something or other. That is the kind of answer we get to a serious suggestion, made with a view to improving the legislation submitted by the Government. It is comparatively unimportant what view the leader of the Opposition, or the hon. member for St. John, held in the past with regard to women suffrage. The question, as I understand it, is whether it is right and just and in the country's interest that we should extend the franchise to the women in those provinces where the franchise has been granted for provincial purposes. Let us address ourselves for a moment to that question.
The Government manifestly has no lack of confidence in the ability of women to consider and arrive at a fair decision on the issues of the day. The very fact of the Government granting the franchise to certain women is in itself ian admission that they believe the women of Canada are so mentally and morally endowed as to be able to pass judgment on the questions before the country. Now, if some women are capable of doing this, are not all women capable of it? No one 'suggests that the women relatives of soldiers are any different from other women, >so far as (assisting at a general election in this country is concerned. I can see no answer to that proposition; it admits of no debate. If we are to go as far as the Government goes we must, if we are to be consistent, go farther and give the franchise to 'all women who are entitled to it under the provincial law.
This legislation is but another example of the old practice of hon. gentlemen opposite, often done in good faith, because they have done it so often it has become a habit with them, of enacting class legislation. This legislation is but another form of privtilegism; it is the last remove from democracy to give the vote to a mere handful of women and withhold it from the rest, for no reason at all except the flimsy, sophistical reason the Secretary of State has given. Now what is his reason? He says that if we were to 'give the vote to all women, it would he no prize to the soldiers' relatives. Those are not his exact words, but that was his idea, framed in his own beautiful language, which I could not for a moment imitate, and the sophistry of which I trust I never for one moment shall. He says it would be a departure from the compensating feature to the soldiers' relatives. That is to say, all women

are entitled to the vote, but we are withholding it from the majority because we wish to give the privilege to the soldiers' relatives. We wish to show them some favouritism, as a sort of compensation for themselves and themselves alone. That is class legislation; the principle is wrong and vicious. The reason given by the Secretary of State is one that will not stand analysis. Let us give to the soldier or to his relatives anything under heaven that will commence to compensate in any real sense for the sacrifice that they have made, but surely the soldiers' relatives would be the very last to be so unreasonable as to say: "Let us be the dog in the manger. Let us, and us alone, have the vote to which all women are entitled." Wlhy should the women relatives of soldiers be thankful because the vote is kept from other women? The Secretary of State does not rightly understand the womanhood of Canada if he thinks these women will rejoice in the fact of being in a position of .solitary majesty of their own, while t'heir .sisters >are not able to exercise the franchise which they have received. I think my hon. friend had better get some better reason than that, and in all .friendship and courtesy I suggest that he ask that this amendment .stand .for a little while that he may consider it, and if there is an. entire absence, as there seems to be, of any real, cogent reason against the amendment, then let the amendment go through. There is no man more ready to admit the accomplishments of the Secretary of .State than myself, but I do think that for some of the reasons he gives in this House when he goes home at night he must be ashamed; I cannot say in Parliamentary language that I think he should be ashamed of himself, but I certainly do think that he should be ashamed of his reasons. We had the Ross rifle for .a while sending our boys to sleep in France and Flanders, when they should have been, full-blooded boys, and the reason the Solicitor General gave for continuing to supply our men with that rifle was that we were liable for an action for damages if we broke our contract. Then he gave us free wheat, because he wanted peace on earth with the farmers out West. Yesterday he told us he was taking away the vote from people of enemy biTth to protect the State, and when I confronted him with the terms of the naturalization certificate, whereby Canada pledges herself to give all political rights in this coum ry to these men, the only reason he had to give was that in Saskatchewan they did something to
the Chinese, and in British Columbia they did something else. There are four illustrations of reasons that the Secretary of State has put up, and I am bound to do him the compliment of saying they are not worthy of him. I trust he will look into all these matters-the reason of the Ross rifle, the reason of the free wheat, the reason for disfranchising the Germans because they did something to the Chinese, and the reason he gives now that he keeps the vote from all women because he says it would not be any special compensation to soldiers' wives if the rest of Canada got it. I would ask that the matter receive further consideration of the Government, and be not turned down for no reason at all that I can see, except it comes from this side of the House.

I must admit the Secretary of State has made the position of the Government perfectly clear. It is the deliberate intention of this Government in this Bill, as in the Military Voters' Bill, to establish in the Dominion of Canada a. military voting caste, for the purpose of perpetuating the present Government in power. They are dtoing this without any parliamentary authority, and without the authority of the people, and by Parliament which is very little more than half representative. Such an exhibition of autocracy Canada never saw before, and we must take it for granted that a continuation of our hon. friends in their present position will give Canada more examples of autocracy .such as the Kaiser will be glad to hear of.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) stated that these decisions were arrived at in England in the old prehistoric times when women were chattels, and men beat their wives. As a matter of fact, the decision was in 1909 and is quoted in the Appeal Cases.
Amendment, Mr. Neely, declared lost.

In view of the defeat of the amendment moved by my hon. friend from Humboldt (Mr. Neely) and of the objections made to it by the Government, I desire to move the following amendment, which I hope will overcome the objection. I beg to move:
That section 1 be amended by adding- after the word "war" in line 34, the words "or is a natural born British subject qualified as ta age, race, and residence, as required in the case of a male person in such province or in the Yukon Territory."
The effect of that would be to enfranchise every woman who is a natural born

British subject, and get rid of the objection which the Secretary of State made in regard to the woman coming from Sweden, who lived here for a year and had the right to vote.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
It gets rid of the objection as to the anomaly of naturalization, but it does not meet the main points at all, namely, that the whole representative value of the vote is gone, and the line of service and sacrifice is destroyed.
Mr. MARCH,: Referring to the following paragraph, will the Secretary of State tell me what is meant by the words " in any of the military forces." Does it mean the military forces of Britain and Canada alone, or the military forces of the Allies as well.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Not the Allies.
Mr. MARCH,: Why not? We have thousands of Belgians and French who left Canada for the front. Why should not the wives and relatives of these men have the right to vote?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: That is worth considering.
When I brought the matter up first, the Minister of Justice promised me they would have that right.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I will take it into consideration.
Amendment, Mt. McCraney, lost on division.
Ayes 16; Nays 38.

Perhaps the minister
will tell us something .about the words "naval forces" used in paragraph 33a. We have only two warships, or so-called warships. I would like to know what is meant by the qualification, of men serving on the naval forces? Is it confined to men who have been engaged on those two vessels?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Minister of Marine and Fisheries can give more information as to the exact details of the naval forces. My hon. friend is no doubt aware that in addition to the force he has mentioned there are patrol boats in the Department of the Naval Service. Those boats are doing very good service on the ooast of several of the provinces of Canada.

The Canada for instance, was in service .many years before the war. I am not aware that the service on her is any different now to what it was before the outbreak of hostilities. Condi-

tions on the Canada and similar vessels are not changed, so far as I know.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Speaking generally, and subject to fuller explanation by the Minister of the Naval Service. I would understand it to include all those vessels engaged in war service under the direction of the Department of Naval Service.

I feel that I would like to have a little more information on this particular point. As I understand this, boys who enlist in the Naval Service become soldiers or members of the Canadian navy. Many of these are minors. Many of them are trained in Canada. I know that there are many of them in Halifax. On what ground do the Government grant the franchise to the mothers and sisters of these boys who have never left Canada, and refuse the franchise to the mothers and sisters of men who have enlisted and who are at Valcartier or a hundred other places in Canada but who have not left Canada? The female relatives of these men will not receive the franchise, whereas the female relatives of the boys who have enlisted in the navy will. Surely we have sufficient discriminations in this Bill without going to that extent?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There may be something substantial in the argument of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell). His apprehension is quite correct that the female relatives of those who have not left Canada are not included in the words "in any of the military forces, or within or without Canada." It may be that there should be a limitation to make the Act fair. The reason generally for using the words "within or without Canada" with reference to the naval forces is that one man suffers just the same as the other. A man engaged on the sea is not in Canada, strictly, speaking, but he is on the waters surrounding Canada. That is why the Act is drawn as it is. If you used the words "within Canada" you would exclude many of these men who should he included. It may be that there are some who should not be included. If there are such as the hon. gentleman describes who 'are simply in training and who have never been in actual service, it may he that a change should he made in the wording of the clause to exclude tiiem. I will look into it at once.

I am glad my hon. friend is going to do that, and 'I hope he will amend the Act so as either not to exclude some or to include many others. The hon.

gentleman has had pointed out to him the discrimination that is being exercised in favour of certain persons and against many others in Canada. I hope that while the Solicitor ' General is trying to recast this Act, he will see if he cannot make it a little fairer to a great many people in Canada. However, we will have a chance of discussing this after recess.

On section 33B-Provincial disqualifications not adopted:

I think section 33A was under discussion when the committee rose. The hon. gentleman from Carleton raised a question in regard to the second and third last lines of this section, and asked for explanation.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes, we will take it up when the hon. gentleman arrives. I think I am safe in saying that section 33B is the same as section 11, part 1 of the present Act, and consequently had to be inserted here, in order to make it applicable to .the whole measure.
I may be a little short in my ability to follow the reading, but it *does not seem to me that the connection is well established between the first paragraph and the subsequent paragraphs.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I was troubled in the same way when first reading it. The section reads:
No person possessed of the qualifications generally by the provincial law to entitle him to vote at a provincial election shall be disqualified from voting at a Dominion election merely by reason of any provision of the provincial law disqualifying him from having his name on the list or from voting.
The objects of the disqualification are -the four classes described in the paragraphs following,-first, the holder of an office; second, any person employed in any capacity in the public service of Canada; and so on.
I can understand what it means, and I hope the minister Vill not think me pernickety if I say that it does not seem to me to say what it means.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think it is
quite clear. It is precisely the same form as section II of the Dominion Elections Act which reads, leaving out the immaterial words:
No person shall be disqualified by reason of any provincial law disqualifying him, (a) the bolder of any office, (b) any person employed in any capacity in the public service of Canada.
And so forth.
If it lead as the Prime Minister reads it it would be all light. But it does not read that way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think so.
Well, I withdraw my objection.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I read it leaving out the immaterial words.
But when the words are in it does not read in the same sense.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The section
reads:
No person possessed of the qualifications generally required by the provincial law to entitle him to vote at a provincial election shall be disqualified from voting at a Dominion election merely by reason of any provision of the provincial law disqualifying him from having his name on the list or from voting-
(a)	the holder of any office; or
(b)	any person employed in any capacity in the public service of Canada or of the province.
Why does the minister insert there the word "generally?" If the person has the qualifications he has them, and that is all there is about it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We are following precisely the present section in the Dominion Elections Act. It seems 'to me quite plain. No person possessed of qualifications generally which would entitle him to vote shall be disqualified by this provision under 'the provincial law.
It would he better to say: "No person possessed of the qualifications required by the provincial law." There is no general qualification.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
There would be a contradiction in terms if we adopted that suggestion, because the section [then, in effect, would isay: "No person possessed of the qualifications required by the provincial law shall, by reason of some of the qualifications themselves, be disqualified." If he has the general qualifications, this particular section will not disqualify him for Dominion purposes.
On paragraph (f)-Posting proclamation : Mr. MEIGHEN: Under the Alberta and Saskatchewan provisions the list, ias compiled by the enumerators, is posted up

eight days before election day, and we are enlarging that to ten days.

That is all right. Is it under this Bill, or under the Soldiers' Votes Bill, that you take four weeks between nomination and election? The time between the issue of th^ writ and election day will be much longer under these newer conditions than previously, and it is desirable that we should have a much longer time than ten days for the posting of the lists, because the enumerator will certainly require a great deal ol time.
The returning officer will receive his writs, lay out his polling subdivisions and appoint his enumerators. There will then be, possibly, a month before nomination day, and a further period of four weeks after that before the election is held. But the lists should be put up a good deal more than ten,days before the election.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not quite understand why my hon. friend thinks that a longer period between nomination day and polling day should affect this particular provision.

My recollection is that under ordinary conditions a period of five weeks should be sufficient from the issue of the writ to the holding of the poll. Eight or ten days would then ,be all that could be allowed between the putting up of the lists and the holding of the poll-that is, giving the returning officer and the enumerators time to prepare their lists. In view of the fact that in this case time will be necessary to take the soldiers' vote, a period of four weeks is being set between nomination day and election day. Under the circumstances, that is all right; but that very fact should give you a longer period between the issue of the writ and the holding of the poll. Where five or six weeks was formerly sufficient, you now require probably ten weeks. In view of these considerations, you should have the enumerators lists completed and in the hands of the public by nomination day. The old law provided that the enumerators' lists should be posted up in public places the day before nomination day. There was plenty of time between the issue of the writ and nomination day for getting out the enumerators' lists. Even at ten days, therefore, the period between the posting of the lists and the holding of the poll is altogether too short. If you provided that the lists should be posted up the day before nomination day, yon would give your enumerators as much time as they have had
TMr. Meighen.]
hitherto, and the public would have much better satisfaction. The enumerators' lists are of very little use to the Opposition party if they are put up only eight days before the election.
The Government candidate will likely assist in preparing the lists, and he will have access to them, but the Opposition candidate cannot do that. The Government party has all the material, and the Opposition party has not any. For that reason I think that the principle of the law as it stands should stand now; that the lists should oe put up by the enumerators, the day before nomination d-ay.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: It would never do to go that far. My hon. friend's contention is that, whereas five weeks were formerly sufficient between the issue of the writ and the day of the election, more than five weeks will now be necessary, because the period of a week prior to nomination day will not " he sufficient to enable the proclamation to issue.
Certainly.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I think the period of a week is not viery far from sufficient. At. all events, I am informed that the one week will be almost sufficient. It must be remembered that we have already made provision for earlier posting up of the notices- ten instead of eight days before the election.
How long before election, day will the lists issue from Ottawa?-

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Between five and six weeks.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: You adopt the provincial poll.
I am speaking now of a Dominion election.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: But in the Dominion election, the provincial polls are adopted under paragraph (g).

The hon. gentleman will find that the boundaries of the Dominion constituencies do not coincide with those of the provincial constituencies. Moreover, there are provincial polls in Saskatchewan only in the cities and in the country districts the same procedure has to be had as is the case in Dominion elections.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not see how there can be no provincial polls in the country districts.

In Saskatchewan, I understand, the procedure is practically the same as it is in the Dominion. We follow the old Dominion law in respect of rural districts; the polls are laid out at each election, because there are no voters' lists.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: But they know where the polls were in the previous provincial elections.	*

Not always; new settlements are springing up, new conditions have to be met. Of course, the matter is somewhat simplified by having information as to the polls used at the previous election, but in this case much of that information would be lost, because it is six years old.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: It is only two or three months old.

I was thinking of the last Dominion election. In view of the fact that a period of eight or ten weeks is provided between the issue of the writ in Ottawa and the taking of the poll, a much longer time should be given than has hitherto been provided between the posting of the enumerators' writs and the holding of the poll. The law now says that the lists shall be posted up the day before nomination. That should be the law in this case, because the returning officers and enumerators will have just as much time under the amended law as they had before.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
familiar with the working of the Dominion Elections Act in Saskatchewan and has an acquaintance with the kind of constituency where the period required would be the longest. But we worked this out pretty carefully, and we really think that we can bring the election on within six weeks from the date of the issue of the writ. We may be wrong in that, but we cannot be very far out. Every member in the House -is
anxious that the time be no longer than that, if possible; six weeks between the issue of the writ and the day of the election is just about enough of that kind of stress and turmoil. We are going to try to bring it on within that time. It may be that a slightly longer period could be allowed, but it seemed to us that ten days was enough for all that there was to do. Possibly twelve days might bo allowed; we shall consider that.

Under the law as' it
now stands the public are to be in possession of the enumerators' lists at the moment the candidates are in the field. The candidates are in the field one week before election day, and one day before that the lists are to be posted up so that the public shall he in possession of the lists when the candidates formally take the field.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There is no real connection between nomination day and the posting of the writs.

I think the intention
was that when the candidates went into the field, the public should have possession of the lists upon which the voting was to [DOT] take place.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not see the connection between the nomination day and the posting of the lists. I do see that the fullest time possible should be given between the time the lists are posted and election day in order to enable a candidate to reach the electors, to provide for his getting about as much as possible, but I do not -see that nomination day has anything to do with it. I have made a note of the matter to see if we can make the time longer. All we have to do is to add an amendment to this section. There are some other things that have to be changed also.

Act. In section 22, there is a paragraph (b), which is not contained in subsection 4. It may not be necessary, but I am calling attention to the fact that subsection 4 is not actually a reproduction of section 22.

That is section 23 of

I would suggest
that the latter part of section 33B be made a new section. In the same section there axe two separate amendments very much mixed up. The Solicitor General might keep that in mind.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
It may be possible to
have the Act read sections 1, 2, 3, 4, and so on, in which case section 33B can be made a new section. I am not quite sure whether that is possible or not. The usual provisions of a revision will be followed in reprinting the whole Act.
On paragraph :(h)-appointment of enumerators to make lists.

I want to bring to
the notice of the committee the Secretary of State and the Prime Minister, the special conditions with regard to Prmce Edward

Island. In that province we have no lists at all either for Dominion or for provincial elections. We have vote by ballot. A good many years ago we had lists, and I heard the candidates, men in public life at that. time, saying that the preparations of those lists and the revision of them from time to time caused them more trouble and expense than the holding of an election.
But that system was abolished. Since then both Conservative and Liberal Governments have been in power in that province, and the present system works so well that nobody thinks o.f making a change. And I feel that if the Government could see its w.ay dear to leave conditions as they are in that province it would be very satisfactory to the people there. There is no insuperable difficulty in the way, I should think. I w>ais very much impressed the other day by the remarks of the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. MoCraney), who is a moderate and a reasonable man, to the effect that the method provided in this Bill for drawing up the lists was practically the same as that which prevailed in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta some years ago, which was found to lend itself to improper practices, more particularly to what is called the tied ballot. I should be very sorry to see anything like that introduced into Prince Edward Island, where we are getting along first-rate, and where there is n'ot even a suggestion of tampering with the ballot or anything of that kind. I think it would be very unfortunate if we now introduced into the province a system wihidh might give rise to a suspicion of improper practices such .as took place in Saskatchewan and Alberta some years ago.
If we had no lists, no enumerators would be required, and that much money would be saved. It might not amount to a great deal, but it would be a saving just the same. I suppose there are .about 130 polls' in the province, .and there would be an enumerator for each poll, at a cost, say, of $100 apiece, which would not be extravagant. That would .amount to $13,000, which the Government might just as well save. I was speaking to the Secretary of State about this matter the other day, and he spoke very fairly about it, .so far as I could judge, but I know he is a clever man, and, perhaps, he w.as just jollying .me a little. He very fairly .and frankly stated, however, that if the .members from Prince Edward Island supporting the Government took the same view as I did, he would see that present conditions, so far as Prince
Edwiard Island was concerned, continued.
I have spoken to the members from Prince Edward Island supporting the Government, and while they have not given me any definite answer, they have very frankly stated that the enumerators under this Bill would practically be organizers for them.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I cannot agree with
them on that.

The members were not very much interested, but undoubtedly they expected some party advantage from this method which they were unwilling to give up. I have an amendment here that I would commend to my hon. friend the Secretary of State.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
If we were to accept it, the Act would have to be very greatly amended.
Mr. .1. J. HUGHES: All that would be necessary, I think, would be to say that the provisions of this Bill with regard -to the drawing up of the lists by enumerators should not apply to Prince Edward Island, but that every other provision would apply. The procedure there is very simple. An elector presents himself at the polling booth on election day .and asks the deputy returning officer for a ballot, and in ninety-eight cases out of a hundred he is entitled to a ballot. In Prince Edward Island we have a homogeneous population and everybody knows everybody else, and the qualifications are very simple. If the agents of one of the candidates think that the man is not entitled to the ballot, objection is raised, and decided upon right there by the returning officer, and in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred satisfaction is given. If the returning officer has any doubt in his mind he puts the voter under oath. If conditions are left as they are in Prince Edward Island, it could do no possible harm to anybody.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Is it not a fact that under the system which my (hon. friend commends in Prince Edward Island, the candidates themselves are put to the trouble and expense of preparing lists on their own behalf? It is perfectly true, as I understand it, that there are no official lists, but it does become necessary for candidates .at an election in that province really to prepare their own lists.

Yes. But as I have already said everybody there is acquainted with everybody else, and there is no difficulty. The agents of each candidate prepare a small list for themselves, either

typewritten or handwritten, and there is no expense attached to it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Do they not
really have to perform, all the duties which an enumerator has to perform, finding out who are the electors,, where they reside, their names and so forth?

There is no trouble at all about that, because everybody there is acquainted w'ith all his neighbours. The fact that the local government has adopted the system, and that nobody ever thinks of changing it, is the best proof that I can give to the Prime Minister and the committee that it suits local conditions. The present system saves trouble and expense.
Mr. ME1GHEN: The hon. member spoke to me about it, and I said virtually what he reports to the committee. I said that I thought it was a subject on which I might well be advised 'by the members from, that province, Liberals as well as Conservatives. I have not had an opportunity since then to see any of the. other members, but I have made inquiries from other sources, and I find there is this difficulty: If we were adopting entirely the same franchise as before, then in a province like Prince Edward Island, where there is little actual movement in. and out of the population, and where, everybody knows everybody else to a degree that does not obtain, in other provinces, it is conceivable that perhaps the most convenient way would be to do without this. But even under those conditions I can remember hon, members from that province complaining to me at other times that they had to make their own. lists, and that it was a matter of great expense to them. That might not be the case in the constituency of my hon. friend (Mr. J. J. Hughes), but in a constituency like Charlottetown, for instance, I can quite understand that it would put considerable extra expense on a candidate. I can remember that the figure was given to me as over the thousand dollar mark.
But the point is this: The same franchise is not adopted. Everybody of the male sex had the vote before, and it was easy to tell who did not vote, because virtually everybody did. Now it is very different. There may be some disfranchised as aliens, I doubt if there would be many, and there are certainly many of the female sex to be added. There will be many of the female sex who will be entitled to vote, and there will be very many who will not. Consequently, the question as to who votes, and

who does not vote, is a much bigger question and requires more decision now than before. That is why we need the lists, otherwise it will be all left for decision until election day. I have not seen the other members from Prince Edward Island since my hon. friend called on me, but it would appear that it would be in his own interests to have the lists compiled in the same way as in the other provinces. It must do good, as far as it goes. There will' be no extra work done that has not to be done in any event, and the line between the voter and the non-voter of the female sex will be clearly drawn and known before election day.

There is some expense that the candidates have to bear in this way. The official lists would be very useful if they wanted to send reading matter from Ottawa to their constituents, but for the sake of an election they are not so useful. If the Secretary of State cannot see his way clear, or the committee cannot see its way clear, to adopt the suggestion I have made and have no lists or enumerators at all, I have another suggestion, to make. We want to have a fair election, and to take no advantage of anybody, Conservative or Liberal. Let us give the Liberals one-half of the enumerators.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I am sure if my hon. friend will consult the members from Saskatchewan and Alberta, he will find he is quite wrong about that. They will assure him that enumerators are needed, not as organizers at all.
I know that some of my colleagues from Prince Edward Island expect to get some advantage in that way.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: They will be deceived.
They may be deceived. As I understand it, the Secretary of State would not think of the suggestion I have made that we should have one-half of the enumerators?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Neither side will have any. The enumerators will be officials of the country; they will not be officials of either side.
Who will recommend them?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The returning officer appoints them.
Who will the returning officer be?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: His name has not been determined on yet. He will be a very fair man.

I suppose those things cannot be helped. I had. occasion to say a few words on the conscription Bill when it was going through the House, and my idea was then, and it is still, that the best thing to do was to have a general election. I felt that would clear the air better than anything else. I made the statement that if the Government would hold a fair election, and was' returned to power, whether I should be in Parliament or out of Parliament 1 would give them every assistance I could in carrying out the law. I would like to keep my promise in that respect, but it is coupled with a fair election. There will be no difficulty in having a fair election so far as our province is concerned, whatever difficulties may arise in the other provinces where, perhaps, people go to greater extremes. I feel satisfied that if we can have conditions there as we have had them for many years, it would conduce greatly to give our people the impression that we were having a fair election, but if new conditions are introduced, and we have such a system as they had some years ago in Saskatchewan and Alberta, which lent itself to improper conduct in regard to elections and provided facilities for crooked work, I fear our people will come to the conclusion that we are not likely to have a fair election, and may thinx that there will be some improper work carried on. However, I cannot do any more than present my views to the committee, and say that I wish very much the Secretary of State would consider whether my suggestion is or is not practicable. I know it would be possible to carry it out, and 1 believe it would be practicable to leave conditions as they aTe in that province.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There is the very great difficulty that it would leave to election day the determining of who votes as a' woman voter, and who does not. I am afraid it would be a pretty big problem to deal with this on the day of the election. It is very different from what has taken place before.

Before six o'clock, the member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) asked the Solicitor General if the wives, sisters and other female relatives of those who are British subjects and are serving in the French or the Belgian army would have the right to vote, the same as the wives and sisters of those who are serving in the British army. The Solicitor General said he would look into it.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The fact of the matter is that is the way the Bill read in the former draft I prepared, but I made up my mind it would be unfair and dangerous. I thought if it was in the Bill there would be very great objection from the other side of the House. I felt it would be unfair to include it, and I will tell you why. It would be too difficult to ascertain whether the allegation of a person w1k>
wanted to vote was correct or not. For example, how could we find out whether the mam. was serving in the Russian army? There are all manners of population in our western country, and the enumerator might, if he was the least unscrupulous, perhaps encourage some people to think they had brothers or relatives in the Russian army. How could that ever be checked? The same would apply to any other army. We can check them in our own army, or in the British army, and can get their numbers, but if we are going to open it to the Allied armies,
I am afraid it might be subject to very great abuse.

I do not think it would be so difficult. All those British subjects who lived in the cities, such as Montreal, Quebec, or Three Rivers, for instance, are well known. The enumerators could get evidence from persons whose word could be taken or whose oath could be taken.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
There would be cases
of that kind, of course.

The French Consul, for instance, would, know of those men who were British subjects and who enlisted in the - French or Belgian armies. He would know exactly where those men are. I do not see any reason why the wives, daughters, widows and mothers of British subjects who are fighting in the ranks of the Allies should be deprived of their right to vote, if the relatives of other soldiers are granted that right. [DOT]

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
There would be cases
that could be ascertained. In my own constituency I would very much like to have this in the law, because there are many French reservists who have gone over from there. But if you open it to one you must open it to all. If you open it to those who claim they have relatives in the Russian army, the Japanese army, the Roumanian army, or any other army, how could you ever check the claims that will be made? I think it would be impracticable and dangerous.

The burden of proof
would, af course, be upon the applicant.

If a woman could not establish to the satisfaction of the enumerator, or the judge, or whoever it is, that .she is entitled to vote, of course she would be refused. It is better to refuse twenty than to refuse a whole class who are entitled to vote.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: It would be just a matter of credibility, because the applicant would have no way of establishing it, in the majority of cases at all events, except by swearing to it and perhaps getting somebody else (to swear to it. I do not think there would be any documentary evidence that could be produced in one case in a hundred.

There might not be any documentary evidence but they could accept the oaths of people who know them well. I do not think there could be anything like the conspiracy which the hon. gentleman mentions for the purpose of procuring the vote for a man. The list of the enumerator will show that his application for a vote is supported by the oaths of persons who are credible, who have known him for a long time and who believe that he has a right to vote, and the enumerator can thus satisfy himself that the application is correct.

In the Military Service Act the Government is leaving the appointment of certain members of the local tribunals to the judges. I think it would be a good provision to be put in. this Act that the enumerators shall be appointed by the judges. Where there are district judges, they know the people in the different localities very well and I think it would be safer that the enumerators should be appointed by them. They would not be as partisan as if they were appointed by the returning officer, who will be appointed by the 'Government.' The returning officers are generally partisans who are recommended to the Government by the members supporting the Government or the defeated candidates or the persons who hold the patronage. The judges would be more impartial in the appointment of enumerators.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member (Mr. Proulx) has made rather a cruel attack on the fairness of the measure passed by his very distinguished leader and in force for many years. These officials have always been appointed by the Governor in Council or the returning officer. I do not see how the judges could very well come in there. The returning officer is the man who has charge of the constituency for election purposes. He has charge of the

working out of the whole machinery of the Election Act applicable to the constituency. He divides it up into polls, and goes about from place to place and appoints enumera-[DOT] tors. I do not think that as a rule the returning officers are partisan. I may be very innocent, but in two elections I contested, where I was the Opposition candidate, I did. not think that there was any partisanship, and I do not see how there could have been to any great extent. I believe that these men, appointed to' responsible positions, intend to observe their oath of office and to discharge the duties that the oath requires. It would be impracticable to bring the judiciary into this. We had better leave the judiciary out of something.

These officers always belong to the party which has control of the appointments. The enumerators can do more to the detriment of the Opposition party, probably, than the re-9 p.m. turning officers. The returning officer only carries out the law.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney), or the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles), can answer -that better than I, but I think they would say "no" to the allegation of the hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Proulx).

As 'the Secretary of State calls me as a witness, I would say that .in my experience there has always been great difficulty in getting a returning officer. The duties are very arduous as compared with the remuneration. When a returning officer is willing to accept the office, a great part of the clerical work is thrown on the Government candidate. The returning officer does not know the riding as a rule. It is hardly as the Secretary of State has explained-'that he lays out the polls and appoints the enumerators. The whole riding has to be laid out, and men who know the districts have to take the enumerations and they must be partisans, but the Government candidate -has to assume the responsibility -and see that there is a fair election. I w-as glad to hear the -tribute the Secretary of State paid to the persons appointed by the late Liberal Administration.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I think the hon. member (Mr. McCrea) very much over-states the phase of the subject that he is drawing attention to. I think he is multiplying by about ten.
I am stating what the hon. member for Parry Sound said.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I think the hon. member said hundreds instead of thousands. All overseas forces are treated alike. It would be utterly impossible to discriminate between the merits of the men in the overseas forces for the purpose of the franchise just as it is impossible to discriminate between the individual merits of men in Canada. We had to take the class. The relatives of all overseas men will be treated alike.
If it is possible to discriminate between people in Canada and those overseas, is it not quite possible to. discriminate between those in England and those who are in the danger zone at the front?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
We do that. We take
all in England, of course, because they may go from England to Prance any day. It would be impossible to say that only the relatives of those in France should vote, because many of those in England may go to France any day at all.

Many of them will go
at no day at all.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think that is
very likely.

May I ask if the hon.
gentleman's statement as to inability to discriminate between members of the expeditionary force serving overseas will apply to those who are engaged in the Canadian War Office-if that is what you call it [DOT]-in London?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Any who are employed there, who are not members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, would never be included in this Bill.
If they are members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force?.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: If they are members of tthe Canadian Expeditionary Force they will be included. I think a great many of them are returned soldiers who have seen service and are back in that office in London unfit for further military service.

Does it apply to men
who are still within the borders of Canada, who have not left, but who are liable to go at any time now?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

I should think that even if the man. has only got as far as Halifax, the sacrifice made by his wife or mother is as great as the sacrifice made by the wile or mother of the man who is twirling a cane and walking up and down the Strand or Picadilly, and who never goes any further.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There is a very great difference. There is no question as to the man in Canada. We know whether he has gone across the ocean or not. But it would be perfectly impracticable to work it out on the other -basis, and say that the relatives of those who are still in England should have votes, because by the time the enumerator makes up the list these men might have gone to. the front. That is not so in regard to the men in Canada. I would have no objection to giving a vote to the relatives of those who are still in Canada. But there might be an incentive for men to join the force in some capacity, not altogether too bona fide, in order to get the votes. If hon. gentlemen opposite want to enfranchise the female relatives of soldiers in Canada, we will consider it, but I really do not think they want it.

There was some evidence given before the Returned Soldiers' Committee by the Auditor General. Speaking of the investigation into that London office, he told us under oath that it would have saved the country thousands of dollars-I think he said hundreds of thousands-if they put a lot of the men out on the street and got them out of the way.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: What office was that?

I do not know whether it was the Pay Office or what department. I would not like to say at present, hut I can get the information, for the minister. If there are men, there who are not real soldiers, but are just playing at the game, I think the discrimination to which my hon. friend referred should properly be exercised. In order that the matter may come under the observation of my hon. friend, I will send him a copy of that evidence, because my recollection is that the matter was gone into rather in detail, and the statements of the Auditor General were confirmed by the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. R B. Bennett), who, I think, had some personal knowledge of the conditions existing in that office. That occurred only a few months ago.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I think the whole matter has been cured now. It can have no application to this Bill. This Bill deals w!th the members of the expeditionary force. If they were playing at soldiering at that time, they must now be in active service, to come under the provisions of this Bill.
When was it cured?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: When we know there is a disease we immediately cure it.
Not in the case of the Ross rifle.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I have not seen the evidence to which the hon. member refers.
I think this discussion will be dealt with better on some other occasion.

I think the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) is under an entire misapprehension as to the purpose of this Bill, or he would not have brought up the point he mentioned. He must know that this Bill is for the purpose of manufacturing votes for the Government, and he must surely know that the man who is drawing pay, without giving service, under the authority of this Government, is surely more certain to cast his vote for the Government, when the time comes, than the man who is compelled to render service, for which he is paid.

As we are talking on the question of enumerators, I think this is perhaps as good a time as any to talk about the condition of things which this Act is going to introduce into my own province I think the Prime Minister will sympathize with me in the difficulty which I experience in regard to this Act. We have a most happy condition of things in regard to the list in Nova Scotia, and in every other

province, I suppose, as well. There is no such officer as an enumerator in our province, and no disturbing elements about the list. About the first of January in each year a man begins to look around, and see that names are properly put on the list. About the 1st of April, the sheriff's court is through with them, and the list is handed in to the county clerk, certified by the sheriff, and a copy of that list is sent to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. That is done every year in every county in Nova Scotia. The machinery runs along smooth-Ij. The revisers are appointed by the county council, and the town councils and' city councils look after the lists. Nobody complains, and everybody gets his name on the list if he has a right to have it there; and if a name gets on the list when it has no right to be there, it is taken off. When it comes to election time, the returning officer gets this list from the Olerk of the Crown in Chancery at Ottawa, and that is the end of it; nobody interferes with it. Now we are up against a condition of things that we do not know really where we are. I cannot gather from this Bill when the list is to be completed, or whether a complete list is to go to the returning officer who is appointed, say, for my own county of North Cape Breton and Victoria. The Government appoints a returning officer for the county. I do not know where he is going to get his complete list. I find some machinery by which twenty or thirty people will go round the county making lists. I find nothing in this Act providing when they are to begin, or what kind of system is to be followed as to where they shall sit, or how they shall conduct the business, or what opportunity one has for getting a name off or on. I must say to the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State that it is introducing into the province of Nova Scotia a very disturbing element indeed, and one which is capable of creating a lot of confusion. If there is any way by which the present machinery of making the lists can be utilized in Nova Scotia, I am sure it would satisfy the people very much better than this measure. The present officials are not partisan. Whatever the complexion of the council may be in Nova Scotia, whether there is a majority one way or the other, each Councillor has always bean permitted, so far as I know, to name his own officers. If there is a Tory 'councillor for the district, as a rule he has Tory officers, and if there is a Liberal councillor, although there might he & Tory majority in the county, he gats his own officer.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: How is the sheriff ap pointed?

He is appointed by tha provincial government, I never heard any complaint as to him. The county officials have been men of high standing, and I have jjever heard aniy complaint about them. I think the same is true of every sheriff in Nova Scotia. I appeal to the Prime Minister in this matter, and I tell him that if the machinery now in vogue in Nova Scotia for looking after the lists were utilized, every one would know where to go, and how the thing was to be done, and it would work out, I think, very much better. As it stands, I must admit, I do not know where it begins or where it ends. Ait present the lists are to be fixed and tinkered with right down to election day, which must necessarily he unsatisfactory to us who are unaccustomed and unacquainted with anything of that kind.

I ask the Secretary of State if I am right in thinking that in 33 A, the words "who is serving or who has served without Canada" will include those that have been sent home and been honourably discharged?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Oh, yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In regard to
