what_ the member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) has said, I am afraid that the members on this side of the House are not quite so well pleased with the lists in Nova Scotia as he is. I am bound to say that, as far as my own county is concerned, Donald Archibald, the sheriff who acted as returning 'officer in many of the elections and who was final arbiter on the lists, was as fair a man as could he found in Canada, and I have not a word to say against him. As far as I know, the same is true of the present occupant of the office. But I have had reports from gentlemen on this side of the House in regard to some other sheriffs that are not precisely of the same tenor. One hon. gentleman has asserted to me that 192 names were dropped from the lists in his county by the sheriff without his knowledge and after it was supposed that the lists had all been settled. He gave me pretty definite information as to that. My hon. friend knows that for many years past there has been an effort in Nova Scotia to obtain judicial revision of the lists, but that demand has not yet been complied with. I am quite sure, therefore, that the view entertained by members on this side of the House in
regard to the condition of the lists in Nova Scotia is not quite the sarnie as that which has been expressed by -my hon. friend. However, so far as the operation of this Bill is concerned, I do not think that there will he any difficulty. The enumerators will commence work as soon as they are appointed, and their work must he completed under the terms of the Bill as it is at present, at least ten days before election day.
How are they to go on with their work? Are they to have a court, sitting in some particular place? .

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They go on precisely in the same way as they have gone on for the last twelve years in Alberta and Saskatchewan. The provisions of this Bill so far as enumerators are concerned are based on the provisions of the law as it has existed in. those provinces. The only difference is that this Bill provides certain safeguards which have not been enforced in Alberta -and Saskatchewan during the period of twelve yeaTS to which I have referred.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
In Alberta and Saskatchewan there are no lists, but in the other provinces for which we are now preparing new machinery they have lists- in Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. We are giving the enumerators power to recast those lists. What is the object of that? So far as I can see, it is simply, on the one hand, to eliminate the names of those who, according to this Bill, should not be on the lists because of their being of foreign origin; and, on the other hand, to place upon the lists the names of female voters who, under this legislation, will have the right to vote as relatives of soldiers. The enumerators take off names here and put on names there, but as a result of their work there is no official decision; the vote can be challenged at the poll and it is provided that a judicial authority shall afterwards determine whether or not the name was properly put on or taken off the list. If the work of the enumerators settles nothing, what is the use of having the work done? Let the lists be taken as they are. A man goes to the poll to vote; objection is taken to him on the ground that he is of alien enemy birth. If he persists in his claim to the right to vote, he easts his ballot and the question whether or not he had the right to vote will be decided after the election by judicial authority. What is the use of having all this machinery? The great advantage of the lists in all the provinces is that the right



to the vote is settled by the presence of the man's name on the list; no one can be challenged if his name is on the list. It seems to me that this work is of absolutely no use.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is true that there were no lists in Alberta and Saskatchewan; therefore, lists had to be made. It is true, also, that in various provinces of Canada there are no complete lists-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes there are.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There are no complete lists for the purposes of this Act, because names must be added and names must be struck off. It is necessary, therefore, to make new lists. If we had followed in their entirety the provisions of the Act which my hon. friend thought was good enough for Alberta 'and Saskatchewan for twelve years, there might be some ground for complaint. As I understand the law of that province, a man could obtain the right to vote by making 'an -affidavit; there was no appeal against that, and no remedy in respect of it afterwards.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The same as it will be here.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The man went on the list; he disappeared the next day; no one could find him; there was no remedy. Gentlemen from the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan have pointed out that the enumerator there w-as in touch with one candidate and not in touch with another, the result being obvious. If we had adopted the method that my right hon. friend 'thought was* a fair method for 'those two provinces for 12 years, I admit that we might be subject to some animadversion. But we have not done that. We have provided in this Bill that the vote of -any .man whose name gets upon the list through his making an affidavit may be afterwards challenged. Any person who goes on in the regular way is subject to having his right to vote challenged afterwards. So that there is, in effect, ta judicial revision of the lists-'that revision, if any is necessary, is to take place after, not before, the voter has deposited his ballot. The safeguard is the same in one ease as in the other, and that safeguard was absolutely wanting in -the provisions of the Act that my hon. friend kept in force in Saskatchewan for twelve years.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The Act with regard to Saskatchewan- -and Alberta was framed in 1905, when the provinces were

created. We took then the provisions that we found in the existing law. We took them as they were. We could do nothing else. There could be no provincial list, because there was no province.
"Sir ROBERT BORDEN: Why could my right hon. friend not have provided a judicial revision in Alberta and Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
Minister of Labour
speechtext: It can be challenged at the poll.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The list is revised by the judicial authority, and his decision is final.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: If a man is asked on election day to take an oath, he has to do so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
No, he cannot be asked to do that. When the judge is revising the lists, a man may be disqualified, but after his name has been put on the list, there is no challenge; the matter is fixed finally. This- Bill is very complicated, but if I understand it aright, the list will be made by the enumerator. That officer will take the list which is made today, which, would be final and the present law, and will strike off names and add on names, hut the question whether those names have been properly stricken off ot added remains to be decided after the vote has been taken. If that is to be the law, why not leave the lists just as they are? Suppose a man's name is put upon the list by an enumerator, and it so happens that he* was born in an enemy country. He comes to the poll and is challenged. He may claim that he has a right to vote and may ask for a certificate from the enumerator. The enumerator will give him a certificate; his name will go on the list, and his vote will be* taken subject to its being accepted or rejected afterwards by the judge. All

this revision is of no benefit. You will have no saving of time or expense; in fact, you will have all the trouble and expense of the enumeration to reach the same conclusion to which you can attain to-day under the law as it is.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: the point is just this, that the work is 90 or 95 per cent done instead of the judge having to do it afterwards. s,If the right hon. gentleman's reasoning was correct, we might as well never have a list and simply have a challenge on election day. That would mean that the judges of Canada would have to revise 1,750,000 votes, whereas by having lists made up by the enumerators as carefully as their abilities can do it, you reduce to a mere fraction of one per cent the work that a judge would have to do.
What section ,re we at?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Paragraph (h), section 42, at the bottom of page 3.
I did not understand that the former clause was passed.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: We are not passing anything; we are passing from one to another.
They are touching them all.

In regard to the procedure in Alberta, at one time the procedure embodied in this measure was partially followed in that province. The provision was made that the man whose name was not on the list could swear his vote on, and that vote was subject to subsequent adjudication before a court.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: That is in the provincial election only.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Would my hon. friend suggest that we had better have the proposed judicial revision eliminated from this Bill and make it precisely as it is now in Saskatchewan and Alberta?
I do not wish to take the responsibility of introducing the legislation that my hon. friend sees fit to introduce.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend is trying to give suggestions.
The Secretary of State has laid emphasis on the statement that be is following the conditions in Alberta and Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: But providing safeguards.

I am pointing out that, if I understand the matter correctly, he is following conditions as they have been, but abandoned in Saskatchewan and Alberta for reasons that prevail there but that may not be valid in other parts of the country. I am only desirous that there shall not be a misunderstanding on the part of the committee as to the facts of the case, and that the committee -may not be impressed with the idea that the provisions of the Bill are desirable in application throughout Canada because it has been found necessary, owing to special circumstances, to apply them as they are applied in Alberta and Saskatchewan. What did occur in Alberta when the principle that is contained in this Bill was embodied in the provincial law was this: Ballots were tied up vexatiously, for the purpose of improperly influencing the election in this way: A number of votes would be challenged, and they would be tied up. They would not be counted at the general count. Then there would have to be a semi-judicial investigation as to the validity of those votes, and there is always the possibility of manipulating the evidence that might be brought to bear, and if the first count seemed to be to some extent indecisive, then the election had to be fought all over again in the courts in regard to those tied ballots. It was not because the principle was not theoretically sound. The, principle was,theoretically,absolutely sound, but in practice it did not work out properly, and, if I understand the matter correctly, the authorities decided rather to take the chances on the occasional count of a vote that w-as not valid than to prejudice

the conclusion of the whole election by reason of dilatory legal proceedings.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I imagine my
hon. friend has a wider experience as to the effect of such provisions than any other member of this House, and naturally any suggestion that comes from him based upon biis long experience are entitled to very careful consideration. I understand him to state as a result of that experience that the system of judicial revision having been tried, and the system without such judicial revision having been also tried for a number of years, it was found that the latter system was on the whole .the more satisfactory of the two.
The lesser of two evils.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And that for the reason which he states very forcibly, namely, that the uncertainty, the delay and inconvenience attending a judicial revision rather outweigh any danger which might result from the lack of such judicial revision. I shall take his view into very careful consideration, as there is a great deal of force in what he suggests, and his suggestion is based upon a very long experience of both systems. Perhaps the matter might be allowed to stand over for the present, and I will confer with the Secretary of State in regard to it.

I only wished to inform
the committee as to the actual facts of the case, and I was led to do so by what I heard the leader of the Opposition say. I am not sufficiently familiar with the Act to know whether I took the right point or not, but I thought that where provincial lists are adopted, and insofar as they are adopted, it would not be an improvement at any rate to provide for any tying of ballots on account of challenge of those votes which were on a fixed list.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: In so far as the lists are adopted, there is no tying of ballots at all. It is in so far as the lists are changed that there is a tying of ballots.
But not the fixed lists?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No.

I want to make sure that I understand this Bill correctly as it applies to the older provinces, particularly Ontario. The list which will be adopted in tlie province of Ontario, subject to change by reason of this Act, will be that list which was finally revised in the autumn of 1916. The method of that revision is well known. Tiie list is prepared from the assessment

roll, and finally revised on appeal by the county judge, except in cities, where they have registration. Do I understand that that is to be the basis of the list in Ontario, subject to the changes made by the enumerator owing to the provisions of this Act? Voters who are disfranchised under this Act will have their names removed from that list.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There will be
changes resulting from both enfranchisement and disqualification.

And the enumerator will have to add to the list the new voters who are enfranchised by this Act? As I understand the proposition of the Government, so far as the list of 1916 as finally revised in Ontario is concerned, there will be no rejection of ballots, except by the ordinary form of challenge. Under ordinary conditions the scrutineer challenges a vote for any cause. If the voter takes the oath prescribed by law the vote is counted. Under the present law that vote will still be counted. So far as new votes are concerned, which are to be added by the enumerator, if objection is taken to any vote it is placed in a separate receptacle tand not counted, except under proceedings which may become necessary on account of the closeness of the vote. I imagine that what my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) had in his mind w.as that the tied ballot wou_d apply to the fixed list as well, but that is not the ease. There is a good deal to be said, however, for his contention as to the merits of the two methods. Whether more will be gained or lost by placing those challenged ballots in .a separate receptacle, is a question for the committee and the Government to consider very seriously.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There are advantages and disadvantages in both methods.

There is another point in connection with clause 48. As I understand it, the voters' list as finally prepared by the enumerators will not be posted, in Ontario, until ten days before polling day. In the county of South Renfrew, for instance, ten days would not give the candidate an opportunity of any practical value of having in his possession a voters' list, which is a very necessary thing for a candidate to have. In a constituency that is over a hundred miles long, and where the electors, particularly ini winter time, can only be reached by team, it would be impossible to make any use of the voters' list if it were not posted for a longer period

than ten days before polling day. Even in a small constituency it would be very difficult to make practical use of it in such a short time. Of course, the candidate will have in his possession the list of 1916 as finally revised except for the changes to be made by the enumerator, but the names of the women voters who are to be added will not be in his possession, and those are the ones about which he will show a great deal of solicitude, and have probably little or no information.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would point out that the similar provisions in force in Alberta and Saskatchewan provide for only eight days before polling day, and that in a country which some years ago was very sparsely settled, and is not as thickly populated to-day probably, as the portion of Ontario to which my hon. friend refers.
It is eight days before nomination day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, eight days before election day.
The old Act says eight days before nomination day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In the Alberta and Saskatchewan Acts it is eight days before election day, and if their Acts would work satisfactorily under conditions such as I have described, it would seem to me there would hardly be the difficulties that my hon. friend anticipates in the county of Renfrew or in any other county in the province of Ontario. However, the Secretary of State has already said in reply to the hon. member for Saskatoon that we will consider extending that period of ten days, and we are going to consider it.

I have no knowledge of conditions in Saskatchewan and Alberta, but I take it for granted that practically every resident there would have a vote, so that a candidate travelling over a constituency out there would not be likely to miss many voters.
But with this new addition of the women voters the situation will be a little different. You will not be in a position to know, unless you inquire intimately, whether they have relatives at the front. The situation is different from what it would be if you were dealing with men living in the vicinity who you would take it for granted, bad the right to vote.
- Mr. MEIGHEN: There is one matter I want to make clear, because I am very anxious that there should not be any mistake whatever in regard to the meaning of this law,- and I invite the attention of the hon. member for Edmonton to the point. When I stated to him and to the hon.. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) that there were no tied ballots in relation to the lists that are not adopted and fixed, but the tied ballot appertained to the work of the enumerator only, that is true in spirit, but it is not absolutely accurate. In this sense: all the enumerator can do is to add the names of women who aTe entitled to vote. All he can strike off are those who should be struck off for alienage or as conscientious objectors. Suppose he should strike off a name saying that the party was a conscientious objector, and if that were not true the man whose name was so struck off, if he was on the original list, -could go and vote. Then the ballot would go into an envelope and become tied; so that, strictly speaking, a .man on the list might get into the tied ballot list.
The work of the enumerator is subject to the tied ballot system?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There is nothing reviewed by the judge except the work of the enumerator. A man should not he on the list, let us say, because he has moved awiay, but the enumerator cannot strike his name off for that reason, and even if he does the man can vote.

As it is at present in our province, if you are going to move to have a name struck off the list, there is one day in the year on which it can be done and that is the fifth day of March, the day on which the revising hoard meets. You must serve the man with a notice that on that day you are going to move before the court of revision to have his name struck off. In this case the enumerator has the power of the revising board; he has the power to strike a name off. What opportunity do you give any person to be heard, and upon what facts does this enumerator strike a name or names off?,

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: He gets as good evidence as he can get, and he acts on that. But the party do:es not need to appeal, because all he has to do is to go and vote. He can make affidavit that he is entitled to a certificate of refusal, and. he votes.
But his vote is not counted.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: It is caunted, if the judge finds he has the right to vote.
Suppose a hundred, or two hundred, or three hundred names were struck off the list by the enumerator-

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There are only 300 on the list.
I am speaking of the electoral district.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: You have to consider the polling division as the unit.

Say there should be 300 of these men struck off in an ordinary constituency. I want to tell you that if you had to deal with some of the people we have to deal with in the Maritime Provinces, you would know how easily it could be done. These 300 votes would not be counted, they would be placed in envelopes, and would finally reach the judge. Think what a burden that would impose upon the candidate, to bring those 300 witnesses in order to prove they are qualified voters. I confess I never had any experience in preparing lists by enumerators as hon. gentlemen in this House from the West have had, and they would know very much more about it than I do. At the same time, it seems to me it makes the enumerator practically a dictator. That is so repugnant to the ideas we have always had in the East in regard to the preparation of voters' lists, that I view it with the greatest alarm.
I hink of a man, who is always a political supporter of course, being chosen to go around the country and make up a list of the female voters, and who would also be allowed to strike from the list the names of any voters who are aliens, or former aliens, or conscientious objectors. So far as the Maritime Provinces are concerned, I think the number of the aliens and conscientious objectors is practically nil. This enumerator starts to make out a list of the female voters. There seems to be practically no appeal from his decision. He works in the dark, or at night, and anywhere he has a mind to, and strikes off practically whomever he pleases. All we know is that ten days before the election one of these lists is put up in the post office, and that the enumerator is to be at some place for two hours each day after that to listen to objections. But suppose he will not listen to them? It seems to me this work should be done by the same officials who are making up the lists at the present time, at least in the provinces east of the Great Lakes. Almost invariably, these enumerators are representative of both political parties. In, the province of New Brunswick you will find once in a

while a board composed altogether of Liberals or altogether of Conservatives, but that is a very* rare occurrence. Each party has a chance to be heard. Before a man's name is removed he must have notice, and. after the list is made it is posted up and notice given that at a certain time the board will meet to revise it. I should think some arrangement of that sort might be arrived at. They have had this system of enumerators in the West, but we have never had it in the East, and I can see all sorts of trouble looming up. I would like the Government to consider if there is not some way of utilizing the machinery already existing for the preparation of those lists.

I would like to
ask the Secretary of State if subsection. 2 so numbered, at the top of page 4, refers to the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan alone.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The four western provinces and Prince Edward Island. Wherever the enumerator makes a whole list, he uses as a basis any information he can get.
If the minister had stated that before, I think it would have cleared up the matter to a great many gentlemen on this side. It would be a very unfair provision to apply in my own province at least.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Why?

I feel very much as my hon. friend does. I had to leave last Friday and I took a copy of the Bill with me. I thought I would have plenty of time on the way down to digest it. I might as well have been reading a Latin grammar that I had never seen as to read that Bill. It was not Latin, it was Greek, to me.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It would have been perfectly plain to my hon. friend if he had had a copy of the Dominions Elections Act with him.
Mr! CARVELL: I did not have a copy of it. If I had had half a day to myself and a copy of the election law, I might have arrived at some conclusion as to what the Bill meant.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think my hon. friend will find that it is not as difficult or complicated as he imagines, when he grasps the basic idea of it, which is that the polling subdivision is the unit for the preparation of the lists in Alberta and Saskatchewan. That law is the basis of this Bill. They adopted the principle in the Act of 1905, based upon a previous Act, that the polling subdivision should be the unit for the preparation of the lists. It rather impressed me with its simplicity, and I do not think it will be difficult to understand this Bill if we keep that idea in mind.
Is it not possible to carry out my suggestion about having the Bill printed?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: It will be possible. I did not want, first of all, to go to the expense, and, secondly, the delay, of printing a large number of copies until we knew what would be its final form.
Only Part II would need to be printed.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
That would not be complete, because Part III is essential to an understanding of the effect of Part II. I intend to have that printed, and indeed we could start to-night and print it, but if we did we would likely have to amend it substantially before it got through committee. I know that the two hon. gentlemen who
have spoken will have no difficulty with a copy of the Election Act before them. I could get on without a copy of the Election Act at all. Certainly, the Bill itself is not very likely to have much meaning without the Election Act read with it.

Some <5f us on this side of the House, with a little labour, could understand the Bill, but a great number would have difficulty in even understanding it. It is only right that they should have some proper understanding of the Bill before they are asked to consider it.

I would like to back up the suggestion made by tihe hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) with regard to the machinery in connection with this Act. It is all very well for the Prime
10 p.m. Minister to say that it is based on the polling subdivision. Let me state what that would mean, and for the purposes oif my illustration I will take the riding of West Middlesex in which there are eighty polling subdivisions. It means that you will have to appoint eighty enumerators in that riding, and that they will have to sit for ten days .before polling day to prepare these lists. That is going to put an immense expense upon -the country. In the 234 ridings, supposing there are eighty subdivisions in each and you have an enumerator for each polling subdivision, the expense is going to be very heavy. /1 think it would simplify matters if this provision of the Act were reversed. The suggestion made by the hon. member for Carleton is sensible and practical. He says: Why not use the present machinery? Speaking of Ontario particularly, this work might be left to the township and municipal clerks in each municipality who have the preparation of the lists in charge.
That is not applicable to the Maritime Provinces.

I am speaking of Ontario.
There is no reason why the Act should not be made applicable to Ontario if a more sensible and less expensive method is proposed than the one suggested. In rural and town municipalities-it may not apply to cities-why should not the township and municipal clerks prepare these lists, and, during the ten days when the enumerator sits, why should not the township clerk sit at the township hall and revise the lists in the ordinary way? He is more familiar with the lists than any other person in the county. In West Middlesex there aTe sixteen municipalities, and sixteen township clerks would do the work. Under the sys-

tem suggested by the Secretary of State you will have to appoint eighty or ninety enumerators who. are not familiar with the lists or with the people as the township clerks are. You .save a great deal of expense in not having to appoint all these enumerators, you have the lists perfected, and on election day one man, the deputy returning officer, will do all the work that you are asking the enumerators to do under this Bill. That would simplify the matter very much, and you would be able to carry out the spirit of the Bill much more intelligently and much less expensively than if you adopt the plan suggested by the Secretary of State. That ihon. gentleman said a moment ago that the enumerator would only have the power to add the names of the female relatives of soldiers and strike off the names of people of alien birth and conscientious objectors. He said that he would have no right to strike off a non-resident if he came back to vote. Are we going to have non-resident voters undeT this Act? If a man has gone from West Middlesex to Carleton, say, and is on the voters' lists, although he is living in Carleton, will he be allowed to come back and vote?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes, the law stands in that regard as it was if no Act were passed.

Under the present law he
could not vote at all.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Then, if he cohld not vote at all, he could not vote under this.
I understood the hon. gentleman to say that that man could come back to vote.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I gave that as an illustration. If a man on the list in Ontario cannot, by virtue of the Ontario law vote, because of being a non-resident, although he is on the list, he cannot vote under this Act. I did not know that. If that is the case my illustration has not any force. I will give another. Suppose that the enumerator says that a man is not of age.
He could not do that.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: He could not do that. That man will go on and vote. It does not enable a non-resident to vote if, according to the Ontario law, he cannot vote.

I would like the Secretary
of State to consider the suggestion I made because I think it is far more practicable than the plan proposed.

In suggesting that the township clerks take the place of the enum-
erators who will be appointed for each polling subdivision does my hon. friend (Mr. Rose) propose that the township clerk should go to each polling subdivision within his township and ascertain the names o'f *the women who may be added under this Act?	*

I do not see any reason why he could not. No man is more familiar with that township, and all the persons residing in it, than he is, and if you have, as a protection to the voter, a further pro' vision that the township clerk shall sit in the town for ten days, to have names added to the list or names struck off, I think you have every protection to the voter.

There would not be very much saved, in the matter of expense, if the township clerk had to go around and do the work of the men who were appointed at these various polling divisions to attend to the work. There is another feature of this question; my hon. friend must remember that each township clerk is, first of all, a servant of the township. It might * be that under this Act he would be required to be present at a certain time to investigate conditions at some polling division and at the same time the township council might require his services along some other line. The township is entitled to his services first. The advantage of appointing an enumerator at each poll, in preference to appointing any one man who lives in some particular corner of the municipality, is obvious. Some one man in each polling division would be better acquainted with all the people in that polling division than an outside man could possibly be. I do not think the township clerk of any municipality would know what men were entitled to be placed on the list under this Act in every corner of the municipality. He might know most of them; he might possibly know more than any other one man would, but I do not think he could possibly be as well acquainted with each polling division as some person selected from that polling division.

I am not much concerned about whether we nominate the township clerk, on account of the saving of expense, although I think there is something in that, but I should like to see some public official appointed so that the suspicion of political partiality in the matter will be removed. The township clerk in Ontario has something to do with the preparation of the list. If you take the revising officer, or the revising board as we

call it in New Brunswick, which prepares the list, or if you take the, secretary treasurer in Nova Scotia who,
I understand, prepares the list subject to supervision, you give it a final flavour. T,he people for generations, in the old portions of 'Canada, have been used to having their lists prepared by municipal authority, and while they have their own troubles, and probably some unfairness, yet the system works out very well. They know how to meet one another and how to .argue these matters, i&nd we get a pretty good list, as ia rule. But I view with a great deal of suspicion, in eastern Ontario, the provision by which the Government is going to appoint its own political friends. They will start out to make a list, .and I cannot see, after reading the Bill over hurriedly, any provision by which any person can appeal to that man and have a name added or a name taken off. He can go to them, but there is no provision for .making an affidavit. You can go to a man and say: "Here is 'a certain woman who has a son at the front," .and the official .may say: "No, she has not a son at the front; .he is at Halifax, and I will not put the name on." What is she going to do?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Vote.
Mr. CARVE.LL: Yes, but her vote will not be counted. She has to go before a judge later on.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: But supposing the system in Ontario were adopted, and you had to go to the judge first, and have the name put on, you would be put to the same expense as in-'the other case.

No. The local revision is all done within a very small compass. Yon can get the affidavits of the proper parties, and prove to the municipal authorities that the party is or is not enitled to be placed on the list, and you make your revision beforehand at practically no expense, because it is all done locally in each .municipality-we call them parishes in the East, or polling districts. But when you force them to vote under protest you call it a tied vote. Then the court meets, and you bring all those people to the shire town. In my constituency I might bring people some seventy-five miles to prove whether they bad a right to be on the voters' list. I do not know whether my hon. friend has appreciated whiairthis thing means. If yon change this provision, so that the municipal authorities would re-revise the list, or
add to the revised list, it would be an improvement. If you have municipal authorities in my province, or in any province in eastern Canada, who have the jurisdiction and the right to make the list of male voters, surely you could be able to hand over to the same authorities the power to make the list of female voters. You are introducing something we never heard of before in eastern Canada, and I can see no end of trouble and misunderstanding, and there would be no end of mistakes. An hon. member near me suggests that they will pick out the female voters who will vote the right way. I am not so very much afraid of that in the East, because people are known to one another, and if the different political organizations take hold o.f the thing and work hard enough, and they have an enumerator who is not too violent a partisan, you may get a fair list. But you have always the suspicion that it is not straight, and you may get hold of a political partisan-and I am sorry tc say we have in the East, on both sides of the fence, men who will do things you can hardly imagine-and if you send a man like that around making up the lists by himself, without any one having the right to -go. to him, it will not be fair. He makes up his list, he is the man to whom you must appeal, and he may say, "I will change it," or "I will not change it." It seems to me you will have all kinds of trouble and unfairness under that system, whereas if the old machinery were adopted people will know what they are doing. The hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) referred to subsection 2 which provides that the enumerator has the right to strike a name from the list on the ground that the party was a former alien or a conscientious objector. My friend might say, "Oh, well, if he strikes a man off improperly the man still has the right to go to the tribunal and make an affidavit. But this is so foreign to our ideas down East in regard to removing names from the voters' list that I cannot accept it for a moment. We look upon it as an outrage to strike a man's name from the- voters' list, unless you give him notice.
Surely a man ought to have the right to protect himself. He ought to have the right to say:	I am hot a German; I am
not an Austrian. He ought to have the right to say: I am a person of Austrian birth, but I was naturalized sixteen years ago. Under this Bill you give the political friends of the Government the right to re-

move the name of that man from the list, and he has no alternative but that of swearing his vote. Later he may have to travel fifty or seventy-five miles in order that he may satisfy a judge that he had the right to vote.

Does this Bill
provide that persons qualified to vote under the Military Voters' Act shall have their names added to the list by enumerators:

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No.
The names of a great number of such are not on the roll.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: If a man qualifies under the ordinary civil law, he has the right to go on the list even though he is a returned soldier. But if he does he can vote only once; the Military Voters' Act provides that.
There will be a large number of soldiers in Canada who are not registered but who will be entitled to vote by simply coming to the poll and taking the oath.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Such men could not get on the list in Ontario, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or Quebec on that ground, because the Bill provides that only female relatives of soldiers can get on.

Most of the persons whose names will be removed from the electoral lists by reason of alienage will be found in the western provinces. Why should their names not remain on the lists and the oath be put to them when they come to vote? If they swear that they were qualified prior to 1902, they will be entitled to a vote. If anybody is of opinion that they were not naturalized prior to that date, they may be required to take the oath; if they decline to take the oath they lose the vote. Outside villages or any incorporated town or city in my constituency I should Ibe willing to let the wives, mothers and sisters of soldiers vote without their names being on the lists. They would be wall known in the several communities in which they resided, and if an oath were inserted in the Act which could be administered to those asking for tire right to vote, that would cover the case. In larger places lists could be made.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
On the same principle you might as well not have a list at all. If you do things that way, the whole election will have to be revised by the judges. Good list-making involves this: as much work as possible should! be done before the

contest; everything that can be finally decided should be decided before the contest. Such as cannot be agreed upon is subjected to judicial decision; but let us not leave everything to judicial decision. If every woman could vote by merely swearing that she was the relative of a soldier-and she might so swear quite honestly-thousands of votes might be polled that should not be polled at all.
My suggestion, of course, is applicable only to rural districts, where it would be almost impossible for any woman to claim improperly the suffrage under this Act.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: It is possible to conceive of an enumerator who would defy the obvious rights of a person who should be on the list, but such an enumerator would be notoriously crooked and notoriously stupid. Suppose the enumerator declines to put on Mrs. Smith whose son, everybody knows, is at the front. He could not do more harm to the candidate whom he is supposed tr favour than he does by taking that course. Whenever that becomes known the people begin to feel that they had better vote the other way. It arouses disgust at once.

That is not the way it is done down East. They manipulate the votes not by refusing to put a man on who is entitled to be registered, but by putting on men who are not entitled to be registered. That is where the difficulty comes in.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Then the names are
posted up, the public become aware of the fact, and the same revulsion of feeling sets in. It may be suggested that this provision might be abused on polling day by too many challenges, -but the same check exists in that respect. If people are sworn -recklessly on polling day, it hurts the candidate whose -agent does the swearing.. The friends of those sworn make up their minds that they do not like that kind of work.
I have known votes to- go the other way as a result of instances similar to this; the thing works out all right in the end. It has worked out all right in -Saskatchewan and Alberta, and the people there are not a, bit better than the people down -in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick; the enumerators are not a bit better or -worse. It is in the interests of all concerned that the enumerators do the work in such a way that it will -be acceptable to the public. It is suggested by some hon. gentlemen that we employ the township clerks to assist in making up the lists. The insuperable difficulty in that respect is that a township includes

many polling divisions and yon cannot work this Act out unless you have an enumerator for eadh division. That is the basic principle of the Act. The polling division is the unit and the enumerator attends to that division; he is right there on polling day; he does his work as best he can; he has to make out his certificates of refusals. If we appointed township clerks we would have to have many deputies.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No, the deputy returning officer has not been doing the work all along. The enumerator has been doing the work, or, in the case the hon. gentleman suggests, the township clerk. He knows the lists; he knows Mrs. Smith; he knows why John Brown is off the list. He is in a position, consequently, to do the work well on election day. On the contrary, the deputy returning officer would be a new man on the job. He would have his other duties to attend to, and you could not reasonably heap these new duties upon him.
Very frequently in the West we have to appoint enumerators as deputy returning officers, because there are many districts in which you cannot get two men.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Where there are small polls it might be necessary.
-*r. L. A. LAPOINTE: It is half an hour since my suggestion of this afternoon, that this Bill be reprinted, was endorsed by my hon. friends from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) and Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean).

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: It is half an hour since the Bill went down to be reprinted.

I am glad to hear that the order has been given. We have lost half an hour, because it is difficult to understand this Bill as we have it. I hope that the Secretary of State will present a Bia with a proper classification of the clauses so that we shall be able to understand it. I suggest that we should discuss cne clause at a time, so that everybody will know what is being discussed. I am glad that the Government has acceded to my request to have this Bill reprinted so that it may be presented in proper form.

Perhaps the committee is not. acquainted with all the facts with regard to the ordinary ridings in Ontario. The member for West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) suggests that the township clerks Should prepare the list of names to be added.
If he will think for a moment, I am sure his experience will tell him that the ordinary township clerk has something other to do than the business of a township clerk. In one township the man may be a druggist. The ordinary township-I aan not .speaking about those which are irregularly shaped-is about twelve miles by fourteen miles. Surely you would not expect a druggist or a merchant-and many country merchants are township clerks-to go over an area of twelve miles by fourteen miles in order to ascertain which women in that area may be entitled to be put upon the list under this caption. That would be quite without the mark. Let us consider another fact. The ordinary polling division, at least in my county, comprises at least between 150 and 200 names. If you have an enumerator in that district, he will be able to cast his eye over it and recall the names of the men in that district wno have enlisted. It is then an easy matter for him to tabulate those names and prepare the list. Surely not much expense will be incident to that. As to the question of the enumerator remaining as it were in appeal, the Bill says:
The enumerator shall attend at the time and place so designated for at least two constcu-tive hours on each of said ten days,
And so on. That will not mean much expense. Our hon. friends from the Maritime Provinces speak of all those officers being appointed, as it were, by law. As a matter of fact, in Ontario in many municipalities the same man may not be township clerk for two years running:	He is
simply appointed by the township council or the town council. One man may be assessor this year. He may become disgusted with the smallness of the salary, or he may have some other cares that take up his time, and may give up the position. The assessor is a "come and go" man. Yet the basis of the lists of the whole township comprising 600 or 700 names is prepared by a man who may be an assessor this year and who may never be an assessor again. He is in no sense an official of a Government, either provincial or federal; he is simply the creature of the township council for that year. The ordinary township clerk may be a farmer or a merchant. Surely you can expect an enumerator to put on the names of ten or twenty women in a division that will have from 150 to 200 names when you can trust him to put on the names in a township of 600 or 700 people. The matter is simple. No man in a polling division is going to be so grossly unfair to his

neighbours as to exclude one woman or one girl who may be entitled to vote on account of being a wife or sister of a soldier at the front. As a matter of fact, the names will all be disclosed, because under this measure the man has to post up the list, and if he left one person's name off it would show that he was a partisan, and the mistake would in any event be corrected. Although the system is new in the old-settled districts of Ontario, it is not new in the unorganized districts such as Thunder Bay, Nipissing and parts of Muskoka and Parry Sound. This system of enumeration has gone on in those districts year after year, and I have never heard any complaint about it. The whole system of enumeration is so simple, it will prove so inexpensive, it is so summary and the people are so brought face to face with their individual enumerator, that there can hardly be any cause for complaint. When the facts are realized by hon. gentlemen from the Maritime Provinces-, they will see, that at least in Ontario, the -matter is a very simple one and should commend itself as being perfectly plain.

I understand that the 1916 list is the last revised list we have in On-tar-io. What are the duties of the enumerators that are appointed? Do they simply add the names of the women voters to the list of 1916? Is that list the adopted list, or is there a means of putting qualified voters, other than women, on the list?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: In. Ontario, excepting cities or towns of over 9,000 population, the list, as'prepared in 1916, is final, except that the enumerator may strike off any one because he is an -alien or a conscientious objector and add o-n women- who are- qualified as being relatives of soldiers. He cannot do anything else. Further, as to the suggestion that has been pressed latterly, it may be recalled that Ontario now adopts the enumeration system, They call the enumerator a registrar, but he is an enumerator, in fact, even more so than he is under this Bill, because he is directed by tihe Act to go from house to house and to enumerate the voters. He must go out into -the highways and byways and compel them to go on the list. It is not his duty to sit and wait until -they come to him. We do not instruct the enumerator Iku* he is to do his work. His duties -are so local that it might not be -necessary for him to go ou-t at all, but he must get the names.

The difficulty with accepting the list of 1916 is, I am afraid, that a -great deal of injustice will be done to many electors. The -hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) -mentioned non-residents. Many people move from one county to another, or from one town to another. In Ontario such people cannot vote in the riding they hav-e left, having ceased, to be residents. With us their names -are put on- the list for the place in which they have taken up residence. This is done each year by means of a court of revision. I would lik-e to see a similar provision in this measure by which such men could get on the -lists an the place in which they reside. In the town in which I live there are many qualified voters who will not be on the list at all because there is no machinery provided by which they can get o-n. The enumerator should be given the power -to accept affidavits, as is done in the court of revision in Ontario. By -means of affidavits, or by presence in -a court to which he might go, a man should be able to get on the list. I am sorry to hear that there is n-o provision made by which these people may get on the lists.

As it is decided to have this Bill reprinted, I would suggest th-at where there is -a new section, or where there are one or more words inserted or added to a section, those new words or sections should be put in brackets, so that we shall know exactly what is old and what is new. If there was only a -slight amendment to a section we could pass it very quickly. In that w,ay, by reading section by section, you will find out what is changed. T-h-at is done in the province from which T come. *

Might I draw the attention of the Solicitor General, following out the suggestion of -the hon. member for Montreal, St. James, (Mr. L. A. Lapointe), to the fact that recently the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Roche) submitted to the House amendments to the Dominion Lands Act prepared in very complete form for the information of the members. I do not know whether it is too late now for the Secretary of State to adopt -such a suggestion, but I do wish to say that the form in which the Minister of Interior submitted to the House his amendments to the Dominion Land Act was most complete in t'he information given, both by comparison and by explanation, and I would recommend very strongly that the Secretary of State adopt the same form in regard to this Fran-

chise Act. The Minister of the Interior would be able to explain just what the character of the preparation was. I can assure the minister that to have an amending Bill placed in the hands of members in the form in which the amendments to the Dominion Land Act were prepared would save an enormous amount of time and discussion, and give the members full information in regard to the changes that are being made.

In the province of New Brunswick the local custodian of the lists is the secretary-treasurer of the county, and at every provincial election he is called upon to deliver the voters lists to the returning officer, and on declaration day the returning officer makes a parcel of all these lists and sends them to the Provincial Secretary. We had a provincial election in New Brunswick in the month of February last, and the lists of 1917, which were prepared in 1916, are no longer in the hands of the Provincial Secretary. All that he could give to the enumerator under this Bill would be a copy of those lists. But if that would be satisfactory to the enumerator, well and good.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The lists are now filed with the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, and have become the official lists.
And the enumerator could get them from the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Oh, yes.	Answering
the hon. member for Haldimand, if his suggestion were carried out and the provisions of the western provinces were applied to the province of Ontario, and that would mean making a new list from the ground up, using the old list as a basis only. I fear there would be no justification for that in the province of Ontario. Even if the present law were applied without any new Act at all, it would mean the adoption of the very same lists and the consequences of that adoption. As to the printing of this Bill it seems to ime it would not be impossible to have the amendments in italics, and I will endeavour to have that done.
Is my understanding of the matter correct, that the principle of the tied ballot has been taken from the present law of Alberta, or has it been repealed?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
My understanding is not the same as that of the hon. member for Edmonton. I have not looked at the statute, but my information-and it comes from one
who certainly ought to know-is that the tied ballot exists in provincial elections in Alberta to-day. We have the same principle here, although much enlarged and improved. In Alberta all they can do is to vote on oath, and if they vote on oath that ballot is tied. They cannot challenge a vote, tie the ballot and have it submitted to a judge. We allow that here. In Alberta all that is done with a tied ballot is that some Justice of the Peace tries the case the next day, or within a few days. We subject it to a judge.

I have not had any , experience of the tied ballot since the provincial election of 1905, and my recollections of it may be somewhat at fault, but in Saskatchewan we had the same provision at that time, I suppose, as they had in Alberta, because both elections were being run under the same law. My recollection of it is that any person challenged would have his ballot put in an envelope and it would be laid on one side as a tied ballot. Before the voter left the polling booth he would be handed an appointment by the deputy returning officer naming an hour within a couple of days when he was to appear before one of two Justices of the peace, near the place of polling, and the right of the voter would then he tried out.
I understand from what the Secretary of State says that while this law introduces the tied ballot there is no local tribunal and everything is held up pending a recount. I attended some local tribunals in connection with the elections of 1905. There are always a number of votes tied up, but these cases are very often quickly settled:	to the satisfaction
of all parties before a Justice of the Peace, without any need for referring them to a judge. That is t-o say, the fact that there is the right of examination and of investigation will obviate the necessity of taking an appeal from the local tribunals to the judge. At the last election I had a county 130 miles long and 60 miles wide, with 147 polling places, and nearly 10,000 votes were cast. Under such a system as this Bill provides it would surprise me very much if there were not at least ten per cent of the ballots tied up. The very cumbrous machinery which makes it so difficult for a person whose ballot is tied, and who lives sixty or seventy miles away from a judicial centre, is a great inducement to an opponent to tie up a vote. If there was a local tribunal where both sides could get information, it would settle a great deal of that. I do not like these tied ballots at all, and

the Secretary of State will find that our elections in the West are going to get into a terrible mess if there are one or two thousand votes-and I venture to say that that will occur-which will have to came before the judge for trial. Imagine the examination of several hundreds of people, even in a judicial matter, with other witnesses possibly coming in.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has forgotten, or possibly has not observed, the conditions under which a ballot can be tied. First, the enumerator must have refused a man the right to vote. ' Now those cases would not be many. .
My hon. friend feels that there may be a g-reao many challenged ballots, but there is a great check which never was used in the provincial contest. The agent must take an oath that he has grounds for believing, and dees believe, that the man appearing to vote has not the right to do so, and he must swear to the reasons for so believing. Of course, he may take oath lightly, and there are some who will, and there would then be a number of tied ballots; but I do not think the election will be in a " mess " on that account. It would hurt the candidate if they tied too many ballots. In any event, supposing they did, it simply means there will be some delay until it is decided. In this contest, in war time, there is bound to be many a delay before we know who is elected, because the soldiers' votes count will not be here for many days after.
I apprehend that in this coming contest many a one will not know whether he is elected or not for many days after the election. This is unfortunate, but it is true.

I think this is going to be an uncertain election for probably a month after election day. We will not know absolutely who is elected, and who is not, for perhaps that length of time after the polling day. MJy recollection is that in the election in the city of Prince Albert in 1905, there were over 300 tied ballots.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
There was no check,
though.

Not of this character.
I do not know that the objection is removed very much, because I think if you post up a list and perhaps only ten days before the polling day you have several hundred names -

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Just 300; that is the maximum.

Mr. MeCRANEY: My hon. friend says just 300," but in some places you will have 500, because you are going to take the township as your unit, or something like that, and you will find it necessary to have polling places where there will be only half a dozen, It is just as easy to take 300 votes in one ballot box, as to take 200, if it is a convenient place for voting. You will have some polling places in which there will be a very large number of ballots in one box, and in which 'there must be a tremendous amount of information obtained. I have spoken to the minister with regard to registration in cities, and he expressed the view a few moments ago that it is desirable to have as much finality as possible. Will lie tell me whether he has given consideration to the proposal to have a registration which will be complete with all proper appeals taking place in our cities. Because it is there the great difficulty over this tied ballot will come. There will be more chair lunges and so on on account of lack of information, whereas if the applicants for registration have to take the oath before they come on, it is a very simple matter.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Of course, in Ontario cities is done. The provincial authorities have a regular board on which sits a judge to do this work, and we simply have to adopt the machinery.
That is the registration.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
It is called that. It is really enumeration. In the west, there is no such machinery. We would have to reerect the machinery and would have to constitute the whole board. We would have to apply the law to suit the times and conditions. I think we would be obliged to have something different in each province. In British Columbia for instance, there is machinery for revision, but it is revision by a provincial officer. Of course it would not do to accept that. In Alberta, there is no machinery at all, neither is there in Saskatchewan. I think there is some new machinery in Manitoba, created by a later Act, I am not just sure what it is. It would be much more difficult to do it in the western provinces. I thought of trying to have something in the western provinces similar to what there is in Ontario, but it did not lend itself to the application of that principle nearly so well as it suits Ontario, and we shall use all our means to try to get it in the western provinces as we have it, and trust to the check to safeguard it, and provide for the

revision afterwards. We have not regarded it as vital even if we have to know the result later on in those western constituencies, because the result will be all the more dependable and more correct after the judges revise it.

I do not altogether agree with my hon. friend's statement. I think the fact of having so many ballots tied up, and people going out of town, and so on, means that the result of the revision would make a more unsatisfactory election than if you have the registration under your own officers. It seems to me that if the sections were taken right from the Saskatchewan Act into this Act, and if you appointed your own officers to carry out your own registration, had the same system of appeals and everything else, you would get a satisfactory list, in the cities at any rate.

It is quite evident we cannot make very much progress to-night, and with the new Bill printed and in our possession to-morrow I think we, on this side of the House, will be in a position to contribute more to the passage of the Bill than we can possibly do now. Our last session was very long, and I would suggest to the Secretary of State that the committee rise for the evening. I do not think there is very much to be gained by sitting longer now.

I agree to some extent with the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Mc-'Craney) as to the necessity for some system of registration. I think it should be extended to towns of 2,000 people. I know from my own experience in working on voters' lists in the province of Ontario, if we adopted the lists of 1916 and made no provision whatever for adding names, we should disqualify a good many citizens.

I think the new
law with regard to voters' lists passed by the Ontario Legislature at the last session made some provision along the lines suggested by my hon. friend from Haldimand (Mr. Lalor), and I was a little surprised to hear the Solicitor General state that no such provision was made in this Bill. I thought the tied ballot covered those who tHight move from one constituency to another. If the lists of 1916 are to be used in the province of Ontario, a great many persons outside of the places of 9,000 and over will certainly be disfranchised. There has been a great movement, of population. For instance, people working in munition
factories in towns of less than 9,000 have moved, and will be disfranchised unless some provision is made. I do not see any reason why the tied ballot should not cover cases of that kind. In the rural districts, a great many tenant farmers change in the spring of the year. A man might move just across the line from one constituency into another, and if no provision is made for it, he will have no redress and cannot tender his vote. The towns and cities of 9,000 and over have always had a great advantage over the rural districts in that respect, because they have registration, and their lists are right up to date when the election comes on.
In view of the length of time that has elapsed since the lists were made _ up in Ontario and the great changes that have taken place because of people working in munition factories and other places, I think it is important that an effort should be made to meet this situation.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
My only duty now is to make fully understood the proposals that are made by my hon. friend from Haldimand (Mr. Lalor) and my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland). If their suggestions are carried out it means the making of new lists by enumerators for Ontario outside of the cities commencing right at the very beginning. It means that in any event. It is true, the old lists might be used as a basis, but they would be new lists and the enumerators would have to decide who should go on and who should not, subject to the revision by a judge. Of course, these hon. gentlemen may have had in their minds that you could have a revision first in the counties, the same as in the cities, but you could not because there are not enough judges to have the work done in time to have an election by next March. It is different in the country districts from what it is in the cities. The territory to be covered is too great to enable the people to get there; yon could not do it. The only way to do is to make new lists comnaencing at the beginning and then depending on the tied ballot for a revision afterwards. I am not afraid of the tied ballot. I hope it will not be abused, but still I do not want to resort to It any more than is necessary. The plan of the Bill was worked out and it was realized that in Ontario we would have to put up with the fact 'that there were some people who would be disfranchised. But if we passed no Act at all *that would be the effect of the present legislation. That is the only list there is,

'that is the list in force land we have to abide by it. Of course, it is not impossible to throw away the lists in Ontario, and, commencing at the bottom, make new lists just as we provide in this Act and just as the Ontario Act provides.
It is much more lengthy.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Much more lengthy, and it has its disadvantages as well as its advantages. I readily admit that there are going to be quite a number who will be unfortunate enough to lose their votes, and there will be some who will be fortunate enough to get votes who should not get them. But is it worth while to make such a great change?

I would not suggest tbiat you should do away with the old list 'and make new ones, but I had hoped that there would be some possibility of taking care of the voters who -are shifted around. I think it would be >a mistake to do away with the old lists. It would -be much more satisfactory to use the lists as already compiled.

No very great hardship or injustice would be done to the farming community because the changes are very few. The injustice is going to be done in the towns of less than 9,000 inhabitants. If some provision could be made by which a revision would take place in towns of 2,000 to 9,000 inhabitants it would obviate a very great injustice. In those towns some provision might be made for a revision of the lists before a judge.

The matter that the hon.
member for South Oxford and the hon, member for Haldimand have referred to seems to me can to some extent be remedied. In Ontario, domicile and residence is essential to the privilege of voting. ' If an elector moves around from one township to another the oath requires him to swear that he is domiciled within the district at the time the vote is taken. Surely we accept the principle that where a man has a vote he must not be deprived of that vote. Why cannot a provision he inserted in the Bill that if a man who is qualified to vote except for domicile moves from one part to another he may go back to the place of his former domicile and vote? There is in this Act, and there has been in the Ontario Act, a discrimination against the country districts, although I do not think there is any very grievous feeling about it. There is provision enabling those living in cities

and towns to apply to a judge to have the names of those who have been omitted and those who have become eligible since the last revision put on the list. There is an anomaly in connection with this Bill to which I would direct the attention of the Secretary of State. There are a number of young men-and this condition more generally prevails in the country districts- who were under 21 years of age when the 1916 lists were revised and who have become of age or will become of age between the time that the last lists were revised and the time when it will be necessary to make the new enumeration. It is an unreasonable and unnecessary anomaly to say that the .sisters, mothers .and female relatives of soldiers who. have become of age shall have votes, whereas the younger brothers, who have been, held at home on the farm to enable the older ones possibly to go to the front, are deprived cf their votes. Provision might he made to include the names of such young men as may be of legal age at the time the enumeration is being made. I think it would appeal to every hon. member of this House that, if we extend that recognition to the female relatives, we might fairly extend it to the younger brothers who have come of age since the 1916 voters' lists were revised.

These sam.e points have been argued for a great many years in the legislature of Ontario. No lists can be made under which some person will not be deprived of a vote who under ordinary conditions. would vote. There have been difficulties from time immemorial arising with regard to a man moving from one constituency to another. Provision was made for cheesemakers and clergymen who had moved from one constituency to another.
As to registration in towns of 2,000, I do not know what the situation is now. When I was in the legislature of the province, members objected to registration being extended to the smaller towns on account of the great expense. A man who has not lived in a town or city where there is registration does not understand that he might just as well run an election as a registration. It reminds me of an anecdote told by an ex-Provincial Secretary, of a gentleman whom he approached one day for a subscription to another candidate who was running. This gentleman represented a constituency which only required a candidate to get the convention and his election was assured. When he asked for a little financial aid for a candidate this gentle-

man inquired, " But, has he had hie convention?" and the reply was: ''He is not going to have -a convention; he is a candidate." Then this gentleman said: "What does he need the money for, if he is not going to have a convention?" Hon. gentlemen who are asking for registration may not find it so convenient when they have the registration. I would just about as soon have an election as a registration. One of the difficulties is that the lists are left at loose ends in large towns, and men pay no -attention and make no effort to get on the list until the time -arrives, and then there is a great -struggle to get on the list. Is this not the situation to-day? If there had been no legislation passed in the province of Ontario, and the law stood as it has been for many years, and we were holding an election, now or within two or three months from now, would we not use identically the same lists that would be -used under this Act, except for the new conditions? So that the conditions are unchanged. The lists of Ontario have not been finally revised, -and would . not be revised, under the old conditions probably, until December. An election held before December would- have been held on the list of 1916, just as this election will be held. So that the difficulties outlined by hon. gentlemen are the difficulties which would have -arisen had the law not been changed in Ontario, no matter when you have the election.

In Ontario, where elections have been held when the lists were not completely revised, the lists were used in the townships in which they had been revised. The hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) tells me, not for Dominion elections. I am not talking about that, but I know in certain townships within my cwn riding, where the lists have been revised within 60 days, which is necessary in order that they may be used, the lists of that- current year were used, whereas in the other townships the lists of the previous year we-re used.
Not -many of them are revised at the present time.
Some of them were revised in the first month.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I desire to refer the hon. member for East Middlesex (Mr. Glass) to sections 151 and 152 of the Dominion Elections Act, which provide for residential voting. They are repealed in this Act, consequently the list stands just 360
as it stood for each polling division in Ontario. Though a man may have moved into another division, he still has his vote in the old division.
Where he is on the list?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
That is not fair. Supposing a man had not been on the list any place, and he moves into another riding, the enumerator has not power to put him on. He has only power to put females on.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: That is all.

I have not been influenced by anything said by the hon. member for Haldimand, or the hon. member who has just spoken. It seems to me that I am absolutely right in regard to the clerk doing the work which the hon. gentlemen proposes that the enumerator shall do, and for many reasons. This Government has made a great many sanctimonious protestations that it wants to be absolutely fair, and not partisan in regard to the soldiers' vote and in regard to this Act, and the minister says he is willing to consider amendments. Let me make a suggestion with regard to these clerks as far as Ontario is concerned. The voters' lists of 1916 are to be used in Ontario. How will they prepare the lists? The assessor prepares his assessment roll, and hands it to the clerk. The clerk copies it off, prepares his voters' list, and passes it on, and that voters' list is revised by the judge. The clerk in each municipality has more thorough knowledge in regard to the lists than any other man in the township.
